articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi! 👋  

I'm nyaomaru, a frontend engineer and OSS developer working mostly with TypeScript.

When we need runtime validation in TypeScript, the conversation often turns into this 👇

"Which library should I use?"

  • Zod?
  • Valibot?
  • ArkType?
  • typia?

Or maybe, just write a type guard?

I maintain is-kit, so I think about this boundary quite a lot.

And recently I started wondering

Are we comparing libraries that are actually solving the same problem?

For example, if all I want is this

if (isUser(input)) {
  input.name;
}

do I really need a schema system?

But if I want:

  • structured validation errors
  • transformations
  • parsing
  • schema metadata
  • framework integrations

then a small boolean guard is probably not enough either.

So instead of asking "Which validator is best?", I tried a different comparison.

I implemented the same User validation with:

  • a handwritten guard with a TypeScript predicate
  • is-kit
  • Runtypes
  • Valibot
  • Zod
  • ArkType
  • typia

Then I compiled, tested them against the same fixtures, measured standalone browser bundle size, and ran a small steady-state runtime benchmark.

The hardest part was not making seven validators compile.

It was making seven validators mean the same thing.

Even “a string with at most 100 characters” can describe different runtime contracts.

So, let's look at what each tool is actually buying us. 😺

🧪 The User we will validate

Here is the shared type.

type User = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  age: number;
  role: "admin" | "user";
  tags: string[];
  profile: {
    bio: string;
    active: boolean;
  };
};

And the runtime rules are:

  • id must be a string
  • name must contain 1–100 UTF-16 code units
  • age must be an integer from 18 to 120
  • role must be exactly "admin" or "user"
  • tags must be an array of strings
  • profile.bio must be a string
  • profile.active must be a boolean
  • extra keys are rejected at the root and inside profile
  • values are not coerced

For this comparison, the main input domain is ordinary JSON-decoded data.

That matters because JavaScript can also give us strange things like inherited properties, sparse arrays, symbols, getters, and non-enumerable keys.

We'll come back to those later.

1. ✍️ Handwritten Guard — Sometimes a Guard Is Enough

Let's start with the boring option, a handwritten JavaScript guard with a TypeScript predicate.

No validation library.

const isRecord = (value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown> =>
  typeof value === "object" && value !== null && !Array.isArray(value);

const hasExactKeys = (
  value: Record<string, unknown>,
  keys: readonly string[],
): boolean =>
  Object.keys(value).length === keys.length &&
  keys.every((key) => Object.hasOwn(value, key));

export const isUser = (value: unknown): value is User => {
  if (
    !isRecord(value) ||
    !hasExactKeys(value, ["id", "name", "age", "role", "tags", "profile"])
  ) {
    return false;
  }

  if (
    !isRecord(value.profile) ||
    !hasExactKeys(value.profile, ["bio", "active"])
  ) {
    return false;
  }

  return (
    typeof value.id === "string" &&
    typeof value.name === "string" &&
    value.name.length >= 1 &&
    value.name.length <= 100 &&
    typeof value.age === "number" &&
    Number.isInteger(value.age) &&
    value.age >= 18 &&
    value.age <= 120 &&
    (value.role === "admin" || value.role === "user") &&
    Array.isArray(value.tags) &&
    value.tags.every((tag) => typeof tag === "string") &&
    typeof value.profile.bio === "string" &&
    typeof value.profile.active === "boolean"
  );
};

And then

declare const input: unknown;

if (isUser(input)) {
  input.name.toUpperCase();
}

This is still very good.

For one local boundary, a handwritten type guard has a huge advantage

There is no extra model to learn.

It is just JavaScript runtime checks plus a TypeScript predicate.

But the cost starts to appear when your codebase grows this

isUser;
isProfile;
isRole;
isNonEmptyString;
isAdultAge;
isStringArray;
isApiResponse;
isConfig;
isFeatureFlag;

Now you are not writing "one guard" anymore.

You are maintaining your own tiny guard library.

And this is where the next option starts to make sense. 👍

2. 🔧 is-kit — When Small Guards Become Reusable Building Blocks

This is the problem I built is-kit around.

I didn't want a schema-first workflow for every narrowing problem.

I wanted small guards that stay small, but compose cleanly.

import {
  and,
  arrayOf,
  isBoolean,
  isNumber,
  isString,
  oneOfValues,
  predicateToRefine,
  safeParse,
  struct,
} from "is-kit";

export const isName = and(
  isString,
  predicateToRefine<string>(
    (value) => value.length >= 1 && value.length <= 100,
  ),
);

export const isAge = and(
  isNumber,
  predicateToRefine<number>(
    (value) => Number.isInteger(value) && value >= 18 && value <= 120,
  ),
);

export const isProfile = struct(
  {
    bio: isString,
    active: isBoolean,
  },
  { exact: true },
);

export const isUser = struct(
  {
    id: isString,
    name: isName,
    age: isAge,
    role: oneOfValues("admin", "user"),
    tags: arrayOf(isString),
    profile: isProfile,
  },
  { exact: true },
);

export const parseUser = (input: unknown) => safeParse(isUser, input);

The important part is that the pieces remain normal guards

const names = values.filter(isName);

if (isAge(value)) {
  // value is number
}

That is useful when your codebase already thinks in terms of predicates.

And this is also where I would draw the line.

safeParse() gives a small success/failure result around a guard.

It does not turn is-kit into:

  • a field-level issue system
  • a transformation pipeline
  • a schema metadata system
  • an OpenAPI ecosystem
  • a form integration layer

If those are the actual requirements, I would rather use a schema library than try to make a guard toolkit become one.

One type-level detail also showed up in the verification, struct() and arrayOf() infer readonly structures.

So the runtime shape matches our User, but readonly string[] is not assignable to mutable string[].

That difference is real, and the type tests make it explicit instead of hiding it with a cast. 🔧

3. 🏃 Runtypes — A Validator Object, Not Just a Predicate

Runtypes moves one level further.

Instead of just a boolean predicate, you get a runtime validator object with several ways to consume it.

import {
  Array as RtArray,
  Boolean as RtBoolean,
  Literal,
  Number as RtNumber,
  Object as RtObject,
  String as RtString,
  Union,
} from "runtypes";

const Name = RtString.withConstraint(
  (value) =>
    (value.length >= 1 && value.length <= 100) || "name length must be 1..100",
);

const Age = RtNumber.withConstraint(
  (value) =>
    (Number.isInteger(value) && value >= 18 && value <= 120) ||
    "age must be an integer in 18..120",
);

export const UserSchema = RtObject({
  id: RtString,
  name: Name,
  age: Age,
  role: Union(Literal("admin"), Literal("user")),
  tags: RtArray(RtString),
  profile: RtObject({
    bio: RtString,
    active: RtBoolean,
  }).exact(),
}).exact();

export const isUser = (input: unknown) => UserSchema.guard(input);

export const checkUser = (input: unknown) => UserSchema.check(input);

export const parseUser = (input: unknown) => UserSchema.parse(input);

export const inspectUser = (input: unknown) => UserSchema.inspect(input);

This feels different from a guard toolkit.

A predicate mainly answers

Is this value a User?

A Runtype can also answer that question, but the same object can:

  • narrow with guard
  • throw with check
  • parse with parse
  • expose structured failure data

Also, check() and parse() should not be treated as synonyms.

Runtypes supports parser behavior, and object handling can differ between validation and parsing contexts.

That is exactly the kind of runtime machinery you do not have in a plain predicate. 🏃

4. 🤖 Valibot — Schema Validation With a Modular API

Valibot is where the comparison starts looking more "schema-like".

import * as v from "valibot";

export const UserSchema = v.strictObject({
  id: v.string(),
  name: v.pipe(v.string(), v.minLength(1), v.maxLength(100)),
  age: v.pipe(v.number(), v.integer(), v.minValue(18), v.maxValue(120)),
  role: v.picklist(["admin", "user"]),
  tags: v.array(v.string()),
  profile: v.strictObject({
    bio: v.string(),
    active: v.boolean(),
  }),
});

export const isUser = (input: unknown) => v.is(UserSchema, input);

export const parseUser = (input: unknown) => v.safeParse(UserSchema, input);

This gives us:

  • schema validation
  • type inference
  • structured issues
  • parsing APIs
  • transformation pipelines

But the API is still function-based and modular.

That is a big part of Valibot's design.

Instead of every capability living as methods on large schema objects, you compose independent functions.

That makes tree shaking a first-class part of the normal API.

And unlike a pure schema-only mental model, Valibot also exposes v.is() as a type guard.

So schema validation and ordinary TypeScript narrowing are not mutually exclusive.

One caveat: v.is() is the guard path. It does not expose validation issues or apply transformations like parsing does. 🤖

5. 💎 Zod — When the Schema Is Part of a Bigger Ecosystem

Now Zod.

import * as z from "zod";

export const UserSchema = z.strictObject({
  id: z.string(),
  name: z
    .string()
    .refine(
      (value) => value.length >= 1 && value.length <= 100,
      "name must contain 1..100 UTF-16 code units",
    ),
  age: z.int().min(18).max(120),
  role: z.enum(["admin", "user"]),
  tags: z.array(z.string()),
  profile: z.strictObject({
    bio: z.string(),
    active: z.boolean(),
  }),
});

export type User = z.output<typeof UserSchema>;

export const parseUser = (input: unknown) => UserSchema.safeParse(input);

// This schema has no transforms, so its output type is safe for the input too.
export const isUser = (input: unknown): input is User => parseUser(input).success;

Zod does not expose a built-in is() method, but this adapter can narrow input because this schema has no transforms. With a transforming schema, safeParse().data is the safe typed value: the original input and output types may differ.

Zod is not interesting because it can validate a User.

All of these libraries can do that.

The real value is everything around the schema:

  • form integrations
  • API tooling
  • schema conversion
  • metadata
  • codecs
  • OpenAPI-related tooling
  • framework integrations

If your schema is already becoming part of application infrastructure, that ecosystem matters. 💎

There is one important detail in this sample though.

I did not use this

z.string().min(1).max(100);

Why?

Because our contract says

1–100 UTF-16 code units

Zod's built-in string length checks use Unicode code points, so this sample uses .refine() with JavaScript's string.length to preserve the stated UTF-16 contract. The shared emoji fixture demonstrates why below.

What about bundle size?

It is too easy to write

Valibot is small, Zod is large.

That is not a good 2026 comparison anymore.

Zod also has Zod Mini, which uses a more functional, tree-shakable API.

The bundle table later in this article measures regular Zod, not Zod Mini.

So it should not be read as Valibot versus the smallest possible Zod setup.

Zod can also compile optimized validation logic at runtime with z.compile() and new Function.

I did not enable it here.

That makes this distinction more useful than the broad label “generated validation”

runtime schema compilation
  vs
build-time generation from TypeScript types

That distinction becomes important when we get to typia.

6. 🚢 ArkType — What If the Runtime Schema Looked Like TypeScript?

ArkType has a very different authoring model.

import { type } from "arktype";

export const UserSchema = type({
  id: "string",
  name: "0 < string <= 100",
  age: "18 <= number.integer <= 120",
  role: "'admin' | 'user'",
  tags: "string[]",
  profile: {
    bio: "string",
    active: "boolean",
  },
}).onDeepUndeclaredKey("reject");

export const isUser = (input: unknown) => UserSchema.allows(input);

export const parseUser = (input: unknown) => UserSchema(input);

export const ArkErrors = type.errors;

I like this comparison

z.int().min(18).max(120);

vs

"18 <= number.integer <= 120";

Neither is "better".

They are different ways to express the runtime contract.

If your team already thinks naturally in TypeScript-like expressions, ArkType is very readable.

allows() also works as a type guard.

And calling the schema directly gives you validated output or an error collection.

Another interesting part: ArkType can precompile optimized traversal logic at runtime when the environment allows new Function.

So ArkType is already doing specialization. 🚢

But it is still not the same architecture as typia.

ArkType starts from a runtime type representation.

typia starts from TypeScript types during the build.

7. 🚀 typia — Generate the Validator During the Build

typia is the outlier in this comparison.

import typia, { type tags } from "typia";

type Utf16Name = tags.TagBase<{
  kind: "utf16Name";
  target: "string";
  value: undefined;
  validate: "$input.length >= 1 && $input.length <= 100";
}>;

export interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string & Utf16Name;
  age: number & tags.Type<"uint32"> & tags.Minimum<18> & tags.Maximum<120>;
  role: "admin" | "user";
  tags: string[];
  profile: {
    bio: string;
    active: boolean;
  };
}

export const isUser = typia.createEquals<User>();

export const validateUser = typia.createValidateEquals<User>();

This is not a runtime schema object.

The source of truth is the TypeScript type plus typia's tags.

Then typia's build transform turns

typia.createEquals<User>();

into specialized validation code.

That means there is no general runtime schema interpreter walking a User schema object.

But there is a trade-off

You need build integration.

The current official setup uses TypeScript 7 and ttsc / typia's transform integration.

Stock tsc alone does not run the transform.

In my verification workspace, the first typia build also had to compile a Go source plugin and took several minutes.

That setup cost is not part of the runtime benchmark, but it is absolutely part of the adoption decision.

Also, typia's built-in MinLength / MaxLength did not match our UTF-16 contract.

So I used a custom tag for name.

Again, same-looking validation rule, different semantics. 🚀

😹 Wait, Even "String Length" Was Different?

This was the first test that made me stop.

"😀".repeat(51).length;
// 102

JavaScript's string.length counts UTF-16 code units.

So with our contract

maximum = 100 UTF-16 code units

this should fail.

And it did fail in:

  • handwritten guard
  • is-kit
  • Runtypes
  • Valibot
  • ArkType

But the original Zod and typia samples accepted it.

Why?

Because their built-in length constraints count Unicode code points instead.

For this string

51 emoji
= 51 code points
= 102 UTF-16 code units

Neither behavior is wrong.

They are just different contracts.

And neither one necessarily matches "what a human sees" either, because grapheme clusters make Unicode even more fun. 😹

So I changed the Zod sample to .refine() and typia to a custom tag.

That was probably the most useful lesson in the whole comparison 👇

Equivalent-looking schemas are not automatically equivalent runtime contracts.

So What Are We Actually Comparing?

At this point, these no longer look like seven interchangeable libraries.

They are different runtime models.

Approach Source of truth           Natural success API                       Structured failures       Transformation model       Compilation / build requirement                          
Handwritten guard Type + handwritten check   Predicate                                 Manual                     Manual                     None                                                      
is-kit   Composed guards           Predicate / safeParse                   Basic valid/invalid result Guard-oriented             None                                                      
Runtypes Runtype object             guard / check / parse               Yes                         Parsers                   None                                                      
Valibot   Schema functions           is / safeParse                         Yes                         Schema pipelines           None                                                      
Zod       Schema objects             parse / safeParse                     Yes                         Transforms / codecs       No build transform; optional runtime z.compile()        
ArkType   Runtime type expressions   allows / invocation                     Yes                         Morphs                     No build transform; runtime precompilation when available
typia     TypeScript types and tags Generated predicates / validation results With validation APIs       Build-generated functions Build transform required                              

This is why I no longer like thinking about them as a simple upgrade ladder.

A schema library is not "a better type guard".
A generated validator is not "a better schema".

They solve overlapping problems at different layers.

✅ What Actually Passed?

The complete harness, lockfile, fixtures, probes, and generated result files live in typescript-validator-comparison. The article links to that immutable commit, rather than to a moving branch.

To reproduce the recorded snapshot:

git clone https://github.com/nyaomaru/typescript-validator-comparison.git
cd typescript-validator-comparison
git checkout --detach b26350d01fd18cb77d55a95e2f3b112657f0d305
corepack pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
corepack pnpm verify

pnpm verify runs lint, strict type checking, fixtures, bundle measurement, benchmarks, JavaScript-only probes, and report generation. The result tables below are that run's saved snapshot, reruns on another machine will naturally produce different timing numbers.

I pinned the versions and ran the same fixture matrix against all seven implementations.

The shared matrix contains 35 JSON fixtures.

That includes:

  • valid users
  • age boundaries
  • name boundaries
  • emoji length cases
  • wrong primitive types
  • missing fields
  • invalid roles
  • invalid array elements
  • extra root keys
  • extra nested keys
  • non-object roots

All seven matched the expected result.

35 fixtures
× 7 validators
= 245 boolean checks

All 245 passed.

The harness also checks input mutation, richer APIs, strict TypeScript compilation, lint, builds, narrowing, and bundled output behavior.

So the implementations agree for the JSON-shaped contract in this article—not necessarily for every JavaScript value.

🧩 One More Surprise: "Exact" Is Not Always Exact

I also tested values outside the normal JSON-shaped input domain. The four probes in the table mean exactly this:

const sparseTags = { ...valid, tags: new Array(2) };
const inheritedFields = Object.create(valid);
const extraSymbol = { ...valid, [Symbol("extra")]: true };
const extraUndefined = { ...valid, extra: undefined };

The repository runs nine more probes, including non-enumerable properties and a throwing getter. Here is what happened for these four

Probe                             Native is-kit Runtypes Valibot Zod     ArkType typia  
Sparse tags array               Accept Reject Accept   Reject   Reject Reject   Accept
All fields inherited             Reject Reject Reject   Accept   Accept Accept   Accept
Extra symbol property             Accept Accept Reject   Accept   Accept Reject   Accept
Extra key with value undefined Reject Reject Reject   Reject   Reject Reject   Accept

All seven accepted the extra non-enumerable property I tested.

All seven threw when reading a getter that throws.

This does not mean one library is "correct" and the others are broken.

It means

"Exact object validation" needs a scope.

For example, my native guard uses

Object.keys(value);

That only sees enumerable string keys.

And this

value.tags.every(...)

skips sparse array holes.

That is perfectly reasonable for JSON data.

It is not a universal policy for every weird object JavaScript can create.

This is another reason I think validator comparisons should state the expected input domain.

📦 Bundle Size

Now the fun table. 😺

Each browser-targeted entry exports only validate.

All of them were bundled with the same esbuild settings:

  • browser platform
  • ESM
  • ES2022
  • minification
  • tree shaking
  • legal comments removed

Then I measured raw, gzip, and Brotli output.

A few important caveats.

This is standalone cost

If your app already ships Zod, the marginal cost of one more schema is not 26 KB gzip.

This table measures isolated entry bundles.

This is regular Zod

Not Zod Mini.

So this table does not answer

Valibot vs Zod Mini?

Generated does not mean zero bytes

typia's final guard bundle was only 772 bytes raw in this test.

But it still shipped generated code and a uint32 helper.

"Generated validator" does not mean "free validator".

Still, the architectural difference is very visible here.

⚡ Runtime

I almost did not include runtime numbers because validator benchmarks get misleading very quickly.
But since the workspace already had the same contract and fixtures, I ran a small steady-state benchmark.

Three cases:

  • valid user
  • wrong id
  • wrong nested profile.active

Each library ran in a separate Node process.

Each case used:

  • 20,000 warmup calls
  • 9 measured samples
  • 50,000 calls per sample

Schemas and validators were created outside the measured loop.

Results are median nanoseconds per call, with min–max in parentheses.

Please do not read this as:

typia is the fastest validator.

This is a microbenchmark.

The same small object shapes are validated repeatedly, so V8 can optimize very aggressively.

I would not interpret a 2.0 ns result as a portable "cost of validation" in a real application.

The success APIs are also different:

  • handwritten guard uses a predicate
  • is-kit uses a predicate
  • Runtypes uses .guard()
  • Valibot uses is()
  • Zod uses safeParse(...).success
  • ArkType uses allows()
  • typia uses a generated equals guard

Those operations do not all perform exactly the same work.

What the benchmark does show is that architecture and failure path matter.

For example:

  • the handwritten guard pays for exact-key checks before rejecting the wrong id
  • ArkType's invalid paths were much cheaper than its valid path
  • typia's generated guard had very low steady-state overhead here
  • Runtypes' richer validation machinery costs more in this particular hot loop

That is useful.

A universal speed ranking is not.

So... Which One Would I Use? 🤔

After doing all of this, my decision tree is actually pretty simple.

Just one local narrowing check?

Use a handwritten guard.

if (isUser(input)) {
  // input is User
}

No dependency is a feature when the problem is small.

Lots of reusable guards?

This is where I use is-kit. 🔧

values.filter(isName);

if (isAge(value)) {
  // ...
}

The problem is not "I need a schema".

The problem is "I keep rebuilding the same predicates and composition helpers".

Want a validator object?

Runtypes is interesting when you like having one runtime object that can: 🏃

guard
check
parse
inspect
assert

Want schema validation with a modular API?

Valibot. 🤖

Especially if client bundle size and tree shaking are important parts of the design.

Want schemas tied into a bigger ecosystem?

Zod. 💎

That is probably its strongest reason to exist in many applications.

And if bundle size is a concern, evaluate Zod Mini separately.

Want the schema syntax to feel like TypeScript?

ArkType. 🚢

"18 <= number.integer <= 120";

is a very different authoring experience from chained schema methods.

Want TypeScript types transformed into validators during the build?

typia.
But I would treat the build integration as part of the decision, not a footnote.

Final Thought

These tools overlap, but they live at different layers.

The hard part is not making seven validators compile. It is making seven validators mean the same thing.

So before comparing package size or benchmark screenshots, ask what the boundary needs to return and what runtime machinery is worth carrying.

Use the smallest model that still represents your boundary well.

Then, which one will you use?

Thank you for reading! 🤲

Green and worthless: what verifying one small application taught me, when an AI agent wrote most of the code.

The Sanity DEV Challenge wrapped up last week, and The Cellar won Path Two. The judges called the build writeup “a study in making verification hard to fake,” which is a generous reading of what was mostly me discovering that my verification was broken.

My submission covered what I built. This is about the part of the build I keep thinking about: how often my checks were wrong.

I spent two weeks building a wine cellar application that can be read at any date in its history. One developer, one agent, about 530 tests by the end. Three of the four real bugs in the project were invisible to every check designed for the feature they lived in.

That was uncomfortable, so I went looking. What I found was worse than missing tests: checks that were green, or red, and meant nothing either way. There turned out to be four distinct ways that happens, and I hit all four in a project where I was being unusually careful.

Lab scientists have had vocabulary for this for a long time. An experiment needs a positive control, proof that your method can detect the effect when it's present, and a negative control, proof that it stays quiet when nothing is there. Each of the four lies below is a missing control, or a control pointed at the wrong thing.

First: the test that cannot fail

No positive control.

The application resolves a wine's drinking window from dated claims. Claims can be proposed by an agent and must be accepted by a person, and a proposed claim is supposed to change nothing until someone accepts it.

That is the load-bearing rule of the whole review workflow, so it got a test. Build the cellar, inject a proposed claim, assert that all 542 bottle states are byte-identical. Green.

It was measuring the fixture, not the rule. Resolution picks the highest authority tier first, then the most recent claim within that tier:

Claim Tier Dated Wins?
The incumbent personal 2024 yes
The one under test personal 2019 no, loses on recency

Both claims are the same tier, so the one under test loses on recency, and it loses whether it is proposed or accepted. Delete the entire review-state filter from the source and the test still passes.

What caught it was a companion assertion written for a different reason: accepting must change at least one state. That one failed, which is how I learned the first one was vacuous.

The rule falls straight out of it. Every test asserting that X has no effect needs a paired assertion showing the effect exists when X is enabled. Without the pair, you haven't tested that X is inert. You've tested that your fixture was inert.

An audit of the rest of the suite found two more of the same shape. One claimed to check that a bottle opened during a period doesn't count as a missed opportunity, but two separate mechanisms excluded that bottle, so the clause under test could be deleted without anything turning red.

I assumed that clause couldn't be isolated and told the agent to fall back to a weaker assertion. It ran the experiment instead, and found a fixture by realizing that "now" in this system is a parameter rather than the clock. As of June 2024, what had I missed that year? is an ordinary question to ask a time machine, and it made the case constructible. The fix was better than the instruction.

All three fixes were verified by mutation: delete the clause the test claims to cover, and watch it finally fail. The original fixture stayed in the suite, renamed to say what it actually tests, because a record of the mistake is more useful than a quiet deletion.

Second: the check that always fails

No negative control.

A week later, building a public static bundle, I added a grep of the built output for leaked API credentials. Five seconds to run, and the failure it catches is unrecoverable, so it seemed like an obvious win.

It fired on every clean build. The pattern was sk[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}, and it matched skipCrossDatasetReferenceValidation, a legitimate export name inside @sanity/client.

This is the mirror image of the first lie, and in practice it's worse. A test that never fails is invisible: nobody notices it isn't doing anything. A check that always fails is noticed immediately, and then it is dismissed, every time, by the person who knows it's a false positive. After a week, the real failure it exists to catch would scroll past with the rest.

A check that always fails certifies exactly as little as one that never can. It just looks more diligent while doing it.

The fix was small. The bound went from twenty characters to forty, which real credentials clear easily and that export name doesn't. Then the scan moved into CI, where it runs on every push instead of whenever someone remembers. A check that always fails is worthless, and a check nobody runs is worth the same.

In control terms, the original grep had no negative control: nothing showing it stays quiet on a build known to be clean. One run against a clean build was all it took to expose it, which is how it was found, by running it rather than shipping it. The other half, proving the tightened pattern still fires on a planted fake credential, is the test I'd add next.

Third: the correct test of a wrong contract

Both controls present, measuring the wrong thing.

This one is the hardest to spot, because there is nothing structurally wrong with the test at all.

The application has a date control spanning 1996 to 2042. Typing a date into it worked for month and day, and the moment you started typing the year, the field snapped back to 1 January 1996. You had to finish with the picker.

The cause is a genuinely surprising piece of browser behavior. A native date input never reports partial text. It reports a complete, well-formed date with the year zero-padded to four digits. Typing 2023 into a field already holding a month and day emits this:

0002-12-31   ->  clamped to the 1996 floor
0020-12-31   ->  clamped to the 1996 floor
0202-12-31   ->  clamped to the 1996 floor
2023-12-31   ->  accepted, but the field was overwritten three keystrokes ago

Every intermediate value is a real, valid date. Every one is out of range. Every one got clamped, and the controlled input wrote the floor back over the edit.

There was a test covering this. It asserted that parseDateInput('1901-01-01') returns the 1996 floor. It passed, and it would have failed if clamping broke. Positive control, negative control, meaningful assertion, all present.

The contract it encoded was wrong. Clamping an out-of-range date is correct when the user has finished entering it and wrong while they're still typing, and the test had no way to know the difference because the specification didn't either.

That's the dangerous category, because the first two look like mistakes once you see them and this one doesn't. An assertion about clamping out-of-range input reads as diligence. It would survive code review. It survived mine. I covered this failure mode in more depth in The Contract Discovery Bottleneck.

Fourth: the right test against the wrong system

Controls present, pointed at something else.

To test the review workflow safely, I set up a staging copy of the dataset. The plan: point the authoring tool and the application at staging, propose a claim, accept it, and watch the right bottles change state, all without touching production.

The authoring tool honored the environment variable that selects a dataset. The application, built by the same command with the same variable set, silently ignored it. Its built bundle was byte-identical to a build with the variable unset, falling back to production. No warning, no error. It built and ran perfectly.

So the authoring tool would have written a proposal into staging while the application reported production. Every number on the screen would have been internally consistent, and about a different cellar.

No amount of rigor in the test helps here. The assertions can be perfect and still certify the wrong thing, because the question that came first, which system am I actually looking at?, was never asked.

The fix had two parts. The application's dataset became a hand-edited literal, so it can't be silently wrong: any change to it shows up in the diff. And the application now displays the dataset name in its header whenever it isn't production. The reasoning matters more than the fix. The question was never how to point it at staging. It was whether I was sure which dataset I had just written to.

The examples are the paths you already walk

Separate from all four, and the one I think about most.

The same date control had an arithmetic bug: the span between 31 January and 1 March computed wrong, because the implementation borrowed days from February and silently dropped the remainder.

I had five verification dates for that feature. They were chosen carefully, from real data, before the code existed. They're the dates in the demo video and the screenshots.

All five passed under the buggy version. The application worked. The screenshots were right. Every date I planned to show anyone was fine.

What found it was a property test across all 17,167 positions the slider can occupy, asserting an identity that has to hold for any pair of dates. The bug lived in a region nobody would drive to on purpose.

Demo-driven verification proves the paths you already walk. That's not nothing, and it's not what you think you're getting.

What actually worked

None of it was "write more tests."

Oracles generated before the implementation, with an explicit instruction not to repair them. Expected outputs computed independently and committed before the code existed. The prompt said to treat them as an oracle rather than as output to be fixed, and to stop and report on any disagreement. When a test fails, the cheapest available move is adjusting the fixture, and that instinct needs to be foreclosed in advance rather than resisted in the moment.

Mutation, but only on the tests that matter. Delete the clause the test claims to cover. If it stays green, the test is decorative. This found two of the three vacuous tests, and the agent started doing it unprompted after the first.

Measurement instead of reasoning, on anything with a number in it. A performance bug hid in four lines of correct-looking memoization that had already passed review. Rebuilding an index cost 6 ms; recomputing the thing the index served cost 0.07 ms. The code memoized the wrong one. Nothing about reading it revealed that. Benchmarking both took ten minutes.

A gate that named what would not count as proof. For checks that needed eyes on a rendered screen, I wrote out the full path being tested and then listed the ways it could be faked: don't satisfy this by calling the module from a script, querying the data another way, or pointing at the test suite. Then: you cannot see a browser, so do not report this as passed. Give me the command, the URL, and the expected numbers, and I'll confirm.

That last one matters more in an AI-assisted build than it used to. A model asked to confirm something it cannot observe is under real pressure to confirm it anyway. The fix isn't trusting it less. It's giving it an honest third answer between passed and failed: not verified, here's how you check. A result nobody could observe isn't a pass, and a harness that can't say so will round it up to one.

Agents are good. They aren't exempt.

The agent wrote nearly all of the code in this project, tests included. So it's worth being plain about who wrote most of the lies above: the same tool that wrote the code they were checking.

That isn't an indictment. Over two weeks the agent was better than I am at a lot of this. Before every stage, it read my specification against the platform and found errors in it; by the eighth session, that pass was turning up ten conflicts at a time, two of them outright mistakes in my spec. When I proposed testing a Function against production with a trigger scoped to a document type that didn't exist, it declined, correctly: scoping a trigger is safe, but the only way to invoke one is to write a matching document, and my plan would have left two permanent mutations in production's history to avoid creating a scratch dataset. It found the fixture I told it was impossible. It measured the cost of a feature I hadn't asked it to measure.

It was also wrong in ways a careful human would recognize. It confidently reported that an API couldn't do something the documentation demonstrated, then fixed it in one line once asked to check rather than assert. It reached the right conclusion about date comparison for the wrong reason, which is right only until the case changes. Asked for a list of the polish work that remained, it drafted the list from the build plan instead of the code, and three of the items were already done. A plan describes work that was scheduled, not work that is left.

And it broke rules. Twice, after being told not to run git commands that change the repository, it ran git checkout to undo its own uncommitted edits. Earlier, it had modified an oracle file it was explicitly told not to touch, then restored it. Every time, it reported the violation unprompted, before I found it. "The agent broke a rule and told me" is more useful data than either cleaner story, "it never broke a rule" or "it broke a rule and I caught it." The rule now says the file tools are the only way to revert anything, including its own edits.

The pattern underneath is the part worth keeping. An agent writes tests the way it writes code: quickly, fluently, plausibly, and from the same understanding of the problem. When one tool writes an implementation and its tests from the same prompt, they share one set of assumptions, and a wrong assumption gets encoded twice and then agrees with itself. That's the third lie, and agents make it cheaper to commit at scale. Speed doesn't remove the verification problem. It moves the bottleneck there, which I've written about before.

What changed the outcome wasn't trusting the agent less. It was making verification structurally hard to fake: oracles committed before the code, controls on every check, gates that named what wouldn't count, and final confirmation in the hands of the one participant with eyes. Under those conditions, the agent didn't just pass the checks. It started improving them.

It happened again

A month later I built a small experiment harness for something unrelated, comparing small language models against plain code on a Raspberry Pi. I knew this taxonomy by then. I found the same lies anyway.

A fixture that couldn't distinguish the behaviors it was meant to compare. A metric that rewarded a model for always giving the safe answer, which is a check that always passes wearing a lab coat. And a missing directory that ran an entire round of questions against an empty reference corpus, producing a detailed, confident, wrong write-up: the right test against the wrong system, again.

Knowing the categories didn't prevent them. It made them faster to recognize, which is the most I'd claim for any checklist.

The honest limit

The oracles catch implementation bugs. They can't catch specification bugs, because I generated them from the same specification.

One of them was stronger by accident. The missed-opportunity oracle used brute-force evaluation of every day in a period, while the implementation used a boundary scan that only evaluates the dates where state can change. Two genuinely different algorithms agreeing is better evidence than one algorithm agreeing with itself, for the same reason a winemaker checks a refractometer against a hydrometer: instruments that fail differently are unlikely to fail together. I wrote about that idea recently, too. But even that oracle shares the specification's assumptions about what a missed opportunity is.

Tests tell you the implementation disagrees with your expectations. They can't tell you whether your expectations deserve to win.

What I'd keep

Four habits, one per lie:

Give every inertness test a positive control. If it asserts that something has no effect, prove the effect exists when it should.

Give every alarm a negative control. If it can't be shown passing on known-clean input, it isn't a check. It's noise with a red icon.

Test properties across the domain, not just the examples. Your examples are the paths you already know work, and the contract is only as good as the cases you thought to ask about.

Verify the target before the result. Make the system under test visible on the screen and in the diff, so "which one am I looking at?" is never a guess.

None of those habits is about AI, and that's the point. The agent made every one of these lies cheaper to commit and faster to find. It didn't change which checks were honest.

The rest is the usual advice, and it wasn't what saved me.

This came out of building The Cellar, an event-sourced wine collection for the Sanity DEV Challenge. The full build is documented in the friction logs in that repository, including every check above and the audits that found them.

articles.title: I built a bot that scans dev.to for phishing comments. It found a coordinated campaign. dev.to banned 70+ accounts.
articles.description: Two weeks ago, a phishing bot commented on my post. Vietnamese text, on-topic, ending with a link to...
articles.body_html:
Two weeks ago, a phishing bot commented on my post. Vietnamese text, on-topic, ending with a link to labagent.tech. Click it and you got a fake dev.to login page.

I reported it. Another appeared. Then another. Same pattern, different accounts, all created the same day.

So I built a scanner. The idea came from Harun (@koda2026), who built the original Tiger Sentinel to protect his own posts. I expanded it into a daily scan.

What it does

Scans dev.to's public API. For each article, fetches comments and scores them against two tiers of signals.

Strong (2+ needed to flag as reportable):

  • Known phishing domains
  • Two or more impersonation phrases ("verify your account", "you have 24 hours")
  • Shortlink + Vietnamese text
  • Shortlink + near-empty comment
  • Shortlink + bot-style username

Weak (review only):

  • Single shortlink
  • Single impersonation phrase

The two-tier scoring is the whole trick. The first version flagged every comment with a link at the end — 313 findings, most legitimate. Requiring two strong signals dropped the noise to near zero.

What it found

First full scan: 500 articles, 313 flags, 4 confirmed phishing accounts.

  • @anh_nguynvn_0478e614ba — 16 comments, labagent.tech
  • @shieldxbot — 12 comments, labagent.tech
  • @suppdevbot — 8 comments, tr.ee + "official platform update"
  • @devantibot — 9 comments, tr.ee + "verify your account"

All four created the same day. All four posting the same pattern. That's a campaign.

The bot groups findings by shortlink domain. That turned 4 accounts into a report:
tr.ee — 2 accounts (phishing)
labagent.tech — 2 accounts (phishing)
tinyurl.com — 25 accounts (coordinated?)
shorturl.at — 23 accounts (coordinated?)
t.co — 20 accounts (likely legitimate)

text

How I reported it

dev.to has a report abuse form at /report-abuse that accepts bulk reports. I sent one submission:

  • The 4 confirmed phishing accounts
  • The 3 domain clusters

Not 199 individual reports. One form, five groups.

What happened

A few days later, all four accounts were gone. dev.to banned them. The tr.ee cluster dropped from 5 to 3. labagent.tech disappeared.

Two weeks later, my account was flagged as Trusted User. The system recognized that my report got a real campaign removed. Future reports now go to the front of the moderation queue.

That's the whole pipeline: Harun's idea → my expanded scan → report → platform acts → trust built.

The lessons

The first version was wrong. 313 flags, mostly legitimate comments. The fix wasn't removing weak signals — it was requiring strong ones to co-occur.

The scanner is not a judge. It produces candidates. A human decides. The 313 → 4 funnel is the point. If a bot reports everything, it reports nothing.

Bulk beats individual. A moderation team processes "4 accounts using the same phishing domain" faster than 199 separate flags.

Continuous beats one-time. Three scans in a row found zero new reportable accounts. That's the success case — no new campaign appeared after the first was removed.

The code

The core scoring function:


python
def score_comment(text, username):
    strong, weak = [], []

    for domain in PHISHING_DOMAINS:
        if domain in text.lower():
            strong.append(f"phishing-domain:{domain}")

    hits = [p for p in IMPERSONATION_PHRASES if p in text.lower()]
    if len(hits) >= 2:
        strong.append("impersonation-pair")
    elif len(hits) == 1:
        weak.append(f"imp-phrase:{hits[0]}")

    short = next((d for d in SHORTLINKS if d in text.lower()), None)
    if short:
        if VIETNAMESE_REGEX.search(text):
            strong.append(f"shortlink+vn:{short}")
        elif len(text) < 20:
            strong.append(f"shortlink+near-empty:{short}")
        else:
            weak.append(f"shortlink:{short}")

    if len(strong) >= 2:
        return "report"
    elif strong or weak:
        return "review"
    return None
That's the whole logic. The rest is pagination, rate limiting, and output formatting.

The takeaway
dev.to is mostly safe. The spam you see is a small number of accounts posting a lot. A coordinated campaign of 4 accounts produced 45 comments across the platform — enough to feel like a flood if you're one of the people getting them, but tiny against the total comment volume.

The report form works. Bulk reporting works. Trusted User status is real and earned by making reports that get acted on.

The scanner is Python on GitHub Actions. I wrote it by describing what I wanted to Google AI Studio and fixing what broke. Not production-grade — no tests, no retries, no alerting. But it caught a real campaign and got it removed.

Credit to Harun (@koda2026) for the original Tiger Sentinel concept. He built it to protect his posts. I turned it into a daily scan.

forkcount.github.io is the calorie tracker I built the same way.

The report abuse form at dev.to is /report-abuse. Bulk submission made the difference.

articles.title: aria-selected on tabs: the selected tab that lies (WCAG 4.1.2)
articles.description: The Notifications tab is open. Its panel is on screen: "Choose which email and push alerts you...
articles.body_html:
The Notifications tab is open. Its panel is on screen: "Choose which email and push alerts you receive." Then VoiceOver lands on the other tab and says Account, selected, tab, 1 of 2, Alert preferences, tab group. On Notifications, the tab you are looking at, it says Notifications, tab, 2 of 2. No selected. The tab you see is not the tab the code says.

WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value has three parts. In E07 (A Custom Div Is Not a Checkbox), a custom control never told VoiceOver it was a checkbox - that was the role. This breakdown is the value. The name and the role are already right here (Account, tab, 1 of 2); the state is wrong.

This breakdown uses the Selected State lab (E10): Case 1 (no aria-selected at all) and Case 2 (aria-selected hard-coded). The evidence comes from real accessibility-tree and VoiceOver captures.

The problem

Case 1 - role="tab" with no aria-selected

The tab list is real: role="tablist" with an aria-label, and two buttons with role="tab". The active tab only gets a different background class. Nothing in the markup says which tab is selected:

<div role="tablist" aria-label="Account settings" class="tab-bar">
  <button type="button" role="tab" id="selected-state-broken-case1-account-tab">
    Account
  </button>
  <button
    type="button"
    role="tab"
    id="selected-state-broken-case1-notifications-tab"
  >
    Notifications
  </button>
</div>

The selection lives in a CSS class. Assistive technology cannot read a class name.

What VoiceOver announced (broken, Case 1)

On first load, with Account visually active:

Account, selected, tab, 1 of 2, Account settings, tab group

You are currently on a selected tab, 1 of 2.

That sounds right, but there is no aria-selected in the markup. The capture notes say VoiceOver may announce selected here without a matching programmatic value in the tree. Do not build on it.

After activating Notifications, with the Notifications panel visible:

Notifications, tab, 2 of 2

You are currently on a tab, 2 of 2. To select this option, press Control-Option-Space.

It is asking you to select the tab you just selected.

What the accessibility tree showed (broken, Case 1)

Captured after activating Notifications:

  • tablist "Account settings", multiselectable: false
  • tab "Account" - focusable: true, selected: false
  • tab "Notifications" - focusable: true, selected: false

Two tabs. Neither one is selected. The screen shows an open tab; the code exposes none. Without aria-selected, the tree's selected state does not track the visual active tab.

Case 2 - aria-selected hard-coded

This is the partial fix. Someone read "add aria-selected" and added it - as literal values:

<button
  type="button"
  role="tab"
  aria-selected={true}
  onClick={() => setCase2Active("account")}
  className={...}
>
  Account
</button>
<button
  type="button"
  role="tab"
  aria-selected={false}
  onClick={() => setCase2Active("notifications")}
  className={...}
>
  Notifications
</button>

The click updates case2Active, which switches the styling and the panel. aria-selected never reads it. On first load that even looks correct, because Account is the starting tab. The bug only shows up when you switch.

What VoiceOver announced (broken, Case 2)

With Notifications focused and its panel visible:

Notifications, tab, 2 of 2

And on Account, which is no longer the open tab:

Account, selected, tab, 1 of 2, Alert preferences, tab group

What the accessibility tree showed (broken, Case 2)

  • tablist "Alert preferences", multiselectable: false
  • tab "Account" - focusable: true, selected: true
  • tab "Notifications" - focusable: true, focused: true, selected: false

The tree agrees with VoiceOver, and both disagree with the screen. Focus moved. Selection didn't.

Why this fails exam-style

  • 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A) requires that the name and role of user interface components can be programmatically determined, that states the user can set can be programmatically set, and that changes to these items are available to assistive technologies. Which tab is selected is a state the user sets by clicking a tab. If the code never updates it, assistive technology is told the wrong thing.
  • The WAS rule for this (Custom Widgets, "Bound ARIA States"): "States such as aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-checked, and aria-pressed MUST update when the UI changes - stale values mislead screen reader users."
  • Case 1 exposes no selected tab: both tabs are selected: false in the tree while one is visibly open.
  • Case 2 exposes the wrong selected tab. The attribute is present and its values are valid, so a quick check for the attribute finds it - but the value is stale.
  • Exam signal for missing state: a tab list where no tab has selected: true while one panel is visible. Exam signal for stale state: selected: true on a tab that is not the open one, often next to focused: true on the tab that is. In both cases, test after switching, and check both tabs - not only the first one.
  • Name and role problems (a control that does not expose what it is) are the E07 side of 4.1.2. role="tabpanel" / aria-controls and arrow-key navigation are separate topics (Panel Association and Full Tabs Pattern labs).

The fix

Bind aria-selected to the same state that drives the active styling and the panel: true on the active tab, false on every other tab. The same fix repairs both cases. In React:

<button
  type="button"
  role="tab"
  id="selected-state-fixed-case1-account-tab"
  aria-selected={case1Active === "account"}
  onClick={() => setCase1Active("account")}
  className={...}
>
  Account
</button>
<button
  type="button"
  role="tab"
  id="selected-state-fixed-case1-notifications-tab"
  aria-selected={case1Active === "notifications"}
  onClick={() => setCase1Active("notifications")}
  className={...}
>
  Notifications
</button>

Without a framework, update the attribute in the same place you switch the tab:

const accountTab = document.querySelector(
  "#selected-state-fixed-case1-account-tab",
);
const notificationsTab = document.querySelector(
  "#selected-state-fixed-case1-notifications-tab",
);

function setActiveTab(id) {
  accountTab.setAttribute("aria-selected", String(id === "account"));
  notificationsTab.setAttribute("aria-selected", String(id === "notifications"));
}

accountTab.addEventListener("click", () => setActiveTab("account"));
notificationsTab.addEventListener("click", () => setActiveTab("notifications"));

Not a CSS class. Not a hard-coded true.

What changed in the tree (fixed)

With the Notifications panel visible in both cases:

  • Case 1: tab "Account" - focusable: true, selected: false; tab "Notifications" - focusable: true, selected: true. The Notifications node lists aria-selected: true, the Account node aria-selected: false.
  • Case 2: tab "Account" - focusable: true, selected: false; tab "Notifications" - focusable: true, focused: true, selected: true.
  • Contrast broken Case 2, where Account stayed selected: true after Notifications became active.

Exactly one tab is selected, and it is the one on screen. The tree finally matches the page.

What VoiceOver announced (fixed)

Case 2, with Account active:

Account, selected, tab, 1 of 2, Alert preferences, tab group

The hint on the active Account tab (Case 1):

You are currently on a selected tab, 1 of 2.

The capture also records a state-only reading for Case 2 (the lab's evidence caption places it on the active Notifications tab):

selected

To be honest about the evidence: the lab capture does not include a full VoiceOver announcement for the active Notifications tab after the fix, so this post does not quote one. The proof for the fix is the tree above - selected: true on exactly the visible tab. While Account is active, the inactive Notifications tab reads:

Notifications, tab, 2 of 2

You are currently on a tab, 2 of 2. To select this option, press Control-Option-Space.

Behaviors to verify

  1. Exactly one tab in each tab list has aria-selected="true"; every other tab has aria-selected="false".
  2. aria-selected reads the same state that drives the active styling and the visible panel - no literal true or false.
  3. Switch tabs, then check the accessibility tree: selected: true must follow the visible tab. Then move VoiceOver to both tabs, not just the first one, and confirm only the open tab is announced as selected. Do not trust a first-load listen.

Practice it

  • Video: https://youtu.be/939KZzpMFuk
  • Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/l2yr49-N8b8
  • Lab: Selected State lab
  • Companion write-up: https://www.wasexamprep.com/go/e10-blog-devto

Takeaway: present is not correct. A tab's aria-selected has to follow the tab that is actually open. Switch tabs, and check the tree, not just your ears.

If this was useful, subscribe to A11Y in Practice on YouTube (@a11yinpractice) for more hands-on accessibility episodes, and visit wasexamprep.com for WAS study notes and labs.

Independent study notes - not affiliated with IAAP or W3C.

articles.title: Day 25–26 of Building Crowdwide — Making the UI Minimal!
articles.description: I was building a social media platform for users to raise their voices. I have made a special...
articles.body_html:
I was building a social media platform for users to raise their voices. I have made a special algorithm for them, and it works really well.

I got suggestions from @akhourianmolkumar, @effessdev, @technogamerz and more users to make the UI minimal.

I was very much interested in adding and showing features to users. Just in that curiosity, I forgot that the UI should be minimal and more comfortable.

I added a huge number of features to the dashboard. Whenever a user opens Crowdwide, they see a bunch of features.

Wherever they check, they get something like a feature.

They scroll, they get a feature.

They click, they get a feature.

They search, they get a feature.

They comment, they get features.

Their posts get reach, they get features.

Even after using Crowdwide for just 5 minutes, they look outside the window and see Crowdwide's features outside there... lol...

So, after noticing this...

I visited some other social media platforms, like Instagram, Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter.

I noticed what they show when users log in.

articles.title: Vite+ 1.0 Is Out. You Don't Need ESLint or Prettier Anymore
articles.description: Do you still need ESLint and Prettier? The team behind Vite+ says no. Vite+ 1.0 shipped on September...
articles.body_html:
Do you still need ESLint and Prettier? The team behind Vite+ says no. Vite+ 1.0 shipped on September 28, and it puts Vite, Vitest, linting, formatting, Git hooks, and Node.js version management behind one CLI called vp and one vite.config.ts.

I wrote about Vite+ back in March when it was still in alpha. It's grown up a lot since then. It's MIT licensed, it's stable, and it's close to 2 million weekly downloads. So I took a small Vue app that uses the usual pile of tools and migrated it to see how much of it Vite+ could swallow.

If you'd rather watch, here's the video:

(Full disclosure: I'm a Developer Advocate at AWS, and Kiro is an AWS product. I use it to finish the migration below, but Claude Code or Codex would do the same job.)

What Vite+ replaces

Vite+ comes from VoidZero, the team behind Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, and Oxc. It isn't a new framework and it doesn't replace Vite. It ties a set of tools together and tests them as one stack, so a single vite-plus dependency takes the place of packages like eslint, prettier, vitest, tsup, and turbo.

The commands map to those tools:

  • vp check formats, lints, and type checks in one pass with Oxfmt and Oxlint
  • vp test runs Vitest
  • vp dev and vp build run Vite 8 with Rolldown
  • vp env manages your Node.js version
  • vp migrate moves an existing project over

The Oxc tools are written in Rust. VoidZero says Oxlint runs 50x to 100x faster than ESLint and Oxfmt is up to 30x faster than Prettier. I didn't benchmark those claims, but I'll share the times I saw later.

Prerequisites

  • macOS, Linux, or Windows. I'm on Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) with Ubuntu 24.04.
  • An existing Vite project. Mine is a Vue 3 app, but React and other frameworks work too.
  • A clean Git working tree. vp migrate edits a lot of files, so commit first.
  • Optional, a coding agent to clean up whatever the migration misses.

The project before Vite+

My test app is a vibe-coded park planner where you save trips and the parks you want to visit. It started out with a pretty typical setup. ESLint for linting, Prettier for formatting, vue-tsc for type checks, Husky and lint-staged for the pre-commit hook, pnpm as the package manager, and separate vite.config.ts and vitest.config.ts files.

That's a lot of config to keep in sync. Here's the scripts block from package.json:

"scripts": {
  "dev": "vite",
  "build": "run-p type-check \"build-only {@}\" --",
  "preview": "vite preview",
  "test:unit": "vitest",
  "build-only": "vite build",
  "type-check": "vue-tsc --build",
  "lint": "eslint . --fix --cache",
  "lint:check": "eslint .",
  "format": "prettier --write src/",
  "format:check": "prettier --check src/",
  "prepare": "husky"
}

Every one of those tools has its own release cadence and its own upgrade guide. I also use NVM to switch Node versions, since I jump between a lot of projects for videos.

1. Install Vite+

On macOS or Linux, run the install script from viteplus.dev:

curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash

On Windows, use PowerShell instead:

irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex

The installer asks if you want Vite+ to manage Node.js for you. I said no to this during the alpha because it fought with my other tools. This time I took the default and said yes. After that, open a new shell (or source your .zshrc) so vp is on your path.

2. Run vp migrate

From the project root:

vp migrate

It walks you through a short list of questions before it changes anything. Do you want pre-commit hooks for formatting and linting? Which agent instructions file should it write? Which editor config? Then it asks whether to migrate ESLint rules to Oxlint (it uses @oxlint/migrate for this) and Prettier to Oxfmt.


vp migrate asks before it converts your ESLint and Prettier configs.

I said yes to the hooks, picked AGENTS.md (Kiro reads it), chose VS Code since the Kiro IDE is built on it, and let it migrate Prettier, ESLint, and the TypeScript shims.

When it finished, I ran the check:

vp check
vp check --fix

vp check found some formatting issues, and --fix cleaned up most of them. A few things were left over. My ESLint rules were now in vite.config.ts under a lint block, and eslint.config.ts was gone. But vitest.config.ts was still around, and there was one lint error it couldn't fix on its own.

VoidZero says up front that larger projects might need a follow-up after vp migrate, so I wasn't surprised.

3. Let your agent finish the migration

Instead of fixing those by hand, I asked Kiro, running Claude Opus 5.5:

I just used Vite+ to migrate this project. Can you complete the migration for Vitest and this error?

If you have Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex open already, I don't see a reason to do this part manually. The AGENTS.md file that vp migrate writes explains the vp commands, so the agent doesn't have to guess. VoidZero also publishes a migration prompt for coding agents, linked from the 1.0 announcement.

It finished in under a minute. It moved the test block from vitest.config.ts into vite.config.ts and deleted the old file. It removed vitest.config.* from the include list in tsconfig.node.json. The lint error was the typescript/no-empty-object-type rule in env.d.ts. It fixed it by changing DefineComponent<{}, {}, unknown> to DefineComponent<object, object, unknown>.

Then I ran the check again:


Formatting, linting, and type checks in one command.

All 39 files were formatted correctly in 731ms, and it found no warnings, lint errors, or type errors in 27 files in 782ms. All 16 tests passed with vp test, and the dev server still ran after a restart.

4. Replace Husky with Vite+ hooks

package.json still had "prepare": "husky", so I asked Kiro to move that over too. Vite+ has its own hooks now. vp hooks sets up Git hooks, and vp staged runs your checks on staged files only.

Kiro removed the .husky/ folder, added a staged block to vite.config.ts, and ran vp hooks enable. The hook script lives in .vite-hooks/pre-commit now, and you commit it with the rest of the project.

It also flagged something I would have missed. Husky sets core.hooksPath to .husky/ in your local Git config. Anyone with an existing clone still has that setting, so the new hooks won't install for them until they run this once:

git config --unset core.hooksPath && vp hooks enable

Put that in your PR description if you're migrating a team project.

What's left

After all that, one vite.config.ts holds the linting, formatting, testing, and staged-file config:

Run vp toolchain to see exactly what you're getting. Mine showed Vite 8.3.5, Rolldown 1.2.15, Vitest 5.0.5, Oxlint 1.89.0, Oxfmt 0.74.0, and tsdown 0.23.1, all pinned by the one vite-plus package. That's the upgrade story I like. You bump one version, and VoidZero has already tested those tools together.

For Node, vp env current shows the Node.js and pnpm versions the project resolves to. If something looks off, vp env doctor explains why it picked them.

Rolling it back

This is why you commit before running vp migrate. If it doesn't work out, go back to that commit, delete the new files like AGENTS.md and .vite-hooks/, and reinstall your dependencies. If you let Vite+ manage Node.js, you can switch back to NVM in your shell config.

Wrap up

The migration was pretty painless. vp migrate did most of the work, and the agent cleaned up the Vitest config, one lint error, and the Husky hooks in a couple of minutes. I'm going to start using Vite+ on most of my projects, and I'm happy to drop NVM.

It isn't feature complete. Remote caching, vp release, and vp docs are still on the roadmap. If you're migrating something in production, read the migration guide on viteplus.dev first.

Are you switching? Let me know in the comments, especially if you've tried it on a big monorepo.

Links

  • Vite+ docs
  • Announcing Vite+ 1.0
  • Vite+ on GitHub
  • My first Vite+ post from the alpha
  • Kiro

articles.title: Astro Wellness: The First Project Built Start to Finish by My Agent Team 🏋️
articles.description: Overview   Hey everyone 👋  A few days ago I wrote about the agent team I built for OpenCode:...
articles.body_html:
Overview

Hey everyone 👋

A few days ago I wrote about the agent team I built for OpenCode: a web-developer primary agent and four subagents for UX/UI, code review, SEO and documentation. The obvious question was, does it actually hold up on a real project?

Meet Astro Wellness, a modern, dark and energetic gym template built with Astro and Bulma. It's the first project the whole team took from empty folder to finished, and it's now listed among the official Astro templates: astro-wellness on the Astro portal. I'm still a bit surprised typing that.

Let's dive in! 🤙

What Is Astro Wellness? 🤔

It's a template for a gym, studio or training brand, ready to adopt and customise. It ships with everything you need to go live:

  • Pages: home (hero, stats, services, testimonials), about, services with pricing plans, blog, contact and a custom 404
  • Dark and light mode through Bulma's themes, persisted in localStorage, following the OS preference on the first visit and applied before first paint
  • SPA style page transitions with Astro's ClientRouter, respecting prefers-reduced-motion
  • A Markdown blog on content collections with a typed schema and an auto generated RSS feed
  • SEO ready: per page title and description, canonical URLs, Open Graph, JSON-LD (HealthClub on the home page, BlogPosting on posts), sitemap and robots.txt
  • Strict TypeScript, typed props on every component, and Bulma imported module by module so nothing unused ships The look is a dark theme with an orange accent plus an adaptive light theme, and every design token lives in two clearly documented places, so re-theming the whole site is a quick job. It's MIT licensed, pnpm only, on Astro 7, with a live demo on Netlify.

How the Team Worked on It 👥

Here's the part I wanted to test. If you missed the previous article, the rule in my setup is simple: nobody edits anything in the first pass. Every agent proposes first, I approve, and only then does it apply changes, with each write still behind an ask gate.

web-developer led the build. It explored the project, proposed the structure (pages, layout, data files, components), and implemented it after my OK, then verified with the type check and the build. The strict TypeScript setup and the clean src/data folder for services, team, pricing and testimonials come from its rules about typed props and keeping pages free of complex logic.

ux-ui-expert handled the design system: the dark and orange palette, the light theme flipping every token automatically, responsive behaviour at Bulma's breakpoints, and the details like focus states and reduced motion support. Its rule of using the framework's primitives before custom CSS is why the project styles stay small and prefixed.

seo-expert audited the head, the structured data, the sitemap, the robots file and the social share image. It's also the reason the README tells you to set your real domain before deploying, since the agent flagged it as something only the template user can decide.

code-reviewer went over the changes with its checklist and reported by severity, with concrete fixes I could approve one by one.

documentation-updater kept the repo honest: README, CHANGELOG, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY and AGENTS.md. Its rule of never documenting what it can't verify against the code is exactly what you want from docs that will be read by strangers.

What Worked 👍

The approval gate paid off. On a template that other people will copy, I didn't want surprise edits. Proposals first meant I made the design and architecture calls, and the agents did the heavy lifting.

Specialists beat one big prompt. Having the SEO and docs passes happen as separate reviews, by agents with their own skill and checklist, made the final result more complete than anything I'd have remembered to ask for at the end of a long conversation.

Consistency. Same structure rules, same naming, same quality bar across the whole codebase, because the conventions live in the agent files and not in my head.

It's reusable. The same team can now take on the next template without me rebuilding the workflow.

What Was Harder 😬

I won't pretend it was effortless. The approval flow means a lot of reading and clicking, and for small tasks it's slower than just doing it. Delegation costs tokens and time. And the agents don't replace judgment: decisions like the visual direction, the tone of the sample content and which sections a gym site really needs were mine.

The other lesson is that a template has a different bar than a personal site. People will fork it, so documentation, accessibility and clean defaults matter more than usual, and that's where having dedicated agents for those jobs helped the most.

Try It, Fork It, Break It 🚀

Astro Wellness is open source and free to use for your own gym, studio or training brand:

pnpm install
pnpm dev

You'll need Node 22.22 or newer and pnpm 10+. Edit src/data/site.ts for your identity, swap the sample content, set your real domain in astro.config.mjs, and deploy the dist/ folder anywhere static. The live demo is at astro-wellness.netlify.app, and issues and PRs are welcome.

Final Thoughts 🌟

Having a template accepted among the official Astro ones was a great moment, but the bigger win for me is the proof that the agent setup works on a real deliverable, not just on demos. One primary agent, four specialists, a lot of small approvals, and a project I'm proud to put my name on.

If you try the template, or build your own agent team for OpenCode, tell me how it goes.

Happy coding! ✨
