articles.title: Auto-syncing Tailwind config from Figma variables on every PR
articles.description: A failed Vercel build on a Wednesday afternoon caught my attention. The error log complained about an...
articles.body_html:
A failed Vercel build on a Wednesday afternoon caught my attention. The error log complained about an undefined Tailwind utility class. A designer had renamed a core colour variable in Figma from blue-500 to brand-blue-primary. The design team published the update and pushed the new tokens to our repository. The frontend team pulled the new JSON files. Nobody remembered to update the Tailwind configuration file to match the new token names.

The build crashed because a component was still trying to use bg-blue-500. The token no longer existed in the design system. This happens all the time when you separate your design tokens from your framework configuration. You end up with a manual gap between the JSON file and the actual utility classes your developers use.

I decided to fix this permanently. I wanted a system where updating a Figma variable automatically updates the Tailwind configuration in the same pull request.

The manual mapping trap

Most teams export their Figma variables to a JSON file. They usually dump this file into a tokens folder. Then a developer opens tailwind.config.js and manually maps the JSON values to the Tailwind theme object.

This approach is incredibly fragile. It relies entirely on human memory. When a designer adds a new shade of green, a developer has to remember to wire it up in the config file.

Here is what that manual mapping usually looks like in a typical project.

const tokens = require('./tokens/globals.json')

module.exports = {
  theme: {
    colors: {
      primary: tokens.colors.brand.primary.value,
      secondary: tokens.colors.brand.secondary.value,
      danger: tokens.colors.feedback.danger.value
    }
  }
}

This works fine for three colours. It completely falls apart when you have hundreds of variables across multiple themes. The nested structure of the design tokens rarely matches exactly what Tailwind expects. You also lose the ability to use Tailwind autocomplete properly if the tokens are nested too deeply.

Parsing W3C Design Tokens

Figma variables can be exported in the W3C Design Token format. This is a standard way of representing design decisions in JSON. Every token has a value and a type.

We need a script to read this W3C JSON format and flatten it into something Tailwind understands. Tailwind expects a simple object where keys are the class names and values are the CSS values.

I wrote a Node script to handle this transformation. It recursively reads the token object and builds a flat dictionary.

import fs from 'fs'
import path from 'path'

const tokensPath = path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'tokens/design-tokens.json')
const tokensRaw = fs.readFileSync(tokensPath, 'utf8')
const tokens = JSON.parse(tokensRaw)

function flattenTokens(obj, prefix = '') {
  let result = {}

  for (const key in obj) {
    const value = obj[key]

    if (value && typeof value === 'object' && 'value' in value) {
      const cleanKey = prefix ? `${prefix}-${key}` : key
      result[cleanKey] = value.value
    } else if (value && typeof value === 'object') {
      const newPrefix = prefix ? `${prefix}-${key}` : key
      const nested = flattenTokens(value, newPrefix)
      result = { ...result, ...nested }
    }
  }

  return result
}

const flatColors = flattenTokens(tokens.colors)

This script takes a deeply nested object and turns it into a flat structure. A token located at colors.brand.blue.500 becomes a key called brand-blue-500. This matches the standard Tailwind class naming convention perfectly.

Generating the configuration file

Now we have a flat object of colours. We need to write this object directly into a new Tailwind configuration file.

I prefer generating a TypeScript file rather than a JSON file. This allows us to keep all the standard Tailwind plugins and type definitions intact. We just inject our dynamic colours into the theme extension object.

const configContent = `
import type { Config } from 'tailwindcss'

export const generatedColors = ${JSON.stringify(flatColors, null, 2)}

const config: Config = {
  content: [
    './src/**/*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx,mdx}',
  ],
  theme: {
    extend: {
      colors: generatedColors,
    },
  },
  plugins: [],
}

export default config
`

const outputPath = path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'tailwind.config.ts')
fs.writeFileSync(outputPath, configContent, 'utf8')
console.log('Tailwind config generated successfully.')

When you run this script, it completely overwrites the Tailwind config with the latest tokens. You no longer have to map anything manually. If a designer changes a name in Figma, the script generates a config with the new name.

Automating the sync with GitHub Actions

Running a script locally is better than manual mapping. It is still not fully automated. Developers might forget to run the script after pulling new tokens.

The best place to run this script is in your continuous integration pipeline. We use GitHub Actions to catch token updates and regenerate the Tailwind config automatically.

Whenever a pull request modifies the design tokens JSON file, the workflow triggers. It runs the parser script and commits the updated Tailwind config back to the same pull request.

name: Sync Tailwind Config

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'tokens/**.json'

jobs:
  update-config:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.head_ref }}

      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Generate Tailwind Config
        run: npm run generate-tailwind

      - name: Commit changes
        run: |
          git config --global user.name 'github-actions[bot]'
          git config --global user.email 'github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com'
          git add tailwind.config.ts
          git commit -m "chore: auto-update tailwind config from design tokens" || echo "No changes to commit"
          git push

This workflow completely removes the human element from the synchronization process. The design tokens act as the absolute source of truth. The framework configuration simply reacts to changes in that source.

Catching drift before it ships

This setup solved our Vercel build failures completely.

Now, when a designer renames a token in Figma, the automated system takes over. The pull request contains the updated JSON file. The GitHub Action runs and updates the tailwind.config.ts file.

During the code review, developers can see exactly how the Tailwind classes will change. If a renamed token breaks an existing component, the standard CI tests will catch the missing class name before the code ever reaches the main branch.

You get a clear visual diff of your design decisions right next to your framework configuration. It forces the design and engineering teams to stay perfectly aligned.

The productised approach

Building the CI pipeline and the parser script handles the code side of things. You still need a reliable way to get the tokens out of Figma and into that pull request in the first place.

I built a tool called Design System Sync to solve this exact problem. It is a Figma plugin that exports your design tokens and variables directly to GitHub or Bitbucket. It automatically generates pull requests with clear visual diffs and assigns reviewers. It exports W3C Design Tokens natively so you can feed them straight into the GitHub Action we just built.

You can learn more about the plugin on the website here https://ds-sync.netlify.app?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot and try it out directly from the Figma Community here https://www.figma.com/community/plugin/1561389071519901700?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot.

Connecting Figma directly to your Tailwind configuration saves countless hours of debugging. You stop hunting for missing utility classes and start trusting your design system again.

articles.title: Why Building a Reliable Calendar UI Is Harder Than It Looks
articles.description: In a workforce calendar, shifts, absences, and days off can look like variations of the same event....
articles.body_html:
In a workforce calendar, shifts, absences, and days off can look like variations of the same event. They aren't. A day off belongs to a calendar date; a shift belongs to a span of time. Mixing those rules can move an event to the wrong day without producing an obvious error.

I worked on a workforce calendar using React, TypeScript, and Bryntum. It combined shifts, absences, overtime, and days off from separate services. They looked similar in the calendar, but their date handling and visibility rules were not interchangeable.

A day off that moves to yesterday

Take a day-off record with the value 2026-10-23. Parsing that string as midnight UTC and displaying it in Los Angeles can produce October 22. The browser has converted an instant correctly; the mistake is that a day off was never meant to be an instant.

Input Incorrect interpretation Expected result
2026-10-23 — date-only day off Oct 22 — UTC midnight formatted in Los Angeles Oct 23 — preserve the intended calendar day

A shift timestamp is different: it represents a moment that may be displayed at different local times. We kept those two paths separate. Here's a reduced TypeScript illustration of that boundary:

TypeScript · illustrative example (not production code)

type CalendarRecord =
  | { kind: "dayOff"; date: string }
  | { kind: "shift"; startsAt: string };

function toCalendarEvent(record: CalendarRecord) {
  if (record.kind === "dayOff") {
    // Keep the calendar date as a date, not a UTC timestamp.
    return { kind: "dayOff", calendarDate: record.date };
  }

  // A timestamp represents an instant; localize at display time.
  return { kind: "shift", startsAt: record.startsAt };
}

The important choice is that the date-only branch does not call new Date() or silently apply timezone conversion. In a real application, the downstream rendering adapter also needs to preserve that meaning. I would test the same record across timezones and calendar views, not just test the conversion function in isolation.

The boundary before Bryntum

The services weren't returning one shared event format. We could have mapped each response directly into the calendar, then handled the differences in individual views. I chose a typed application event model instead. It gave IDs, categories, date handling, and permission metadata a consistent shape before anything reached Bryntum.

Where service-specific data stops and calendar rendering begins

SERVICE CONTRACTS
  Shifts · overtime           Absences · days off
  Identifiers and time fields Categories and visibility rules
                 ↓
        Typed application event model
        Stable identity · date handling · categories
        Permission metadata
                 ↓
  Product rules               View adapters
  Normalized events           Day · week · month · team
  Consistent access rules
                 ↓
    Bryntum: event layout, interactions, and presentation

The extra mapping layer meant more code and more tests. The alternative was to maintain the same conversion and visibility logic in several places, including day, week, month, and team views. I preferred one boundary where the behavior could be reviewed and tested.

A responsive calendar still needs fresh data

Calendar navigation creates an awkward balance. People move between weeks and return to ranges they recently viewed. Fetching everything again makes the UI feel slow; never refreshing cached results can leave an old schedule on screen.

Example: moving across weeks, then returning

Step Range Action
01 Week 42 Load the visible range
02 Week 43 Navigate forward
03 Week 42 Reuse cached results; revalidate

We reused loaded ranges, debounced quick navigation, and refreshed in the background when needed. The selected date and view could be restored, but the schedule itself still needed revalidation. Another important check was ensuring a late response from an earlier range could not overwrite the one currently on screen.

What I checked beyond the happy path

A populated calendar isn't proof that its data is right. The cases worth checking were the quiet failures: date-only records shifting days, confidential absence details showing in another view, cached ranges not refreshing, and an old request returning after the user had navigated somewhere else.

What I would carry into the next scheduling project is not a particular calendar configuration. It's the decision to make dates, permissions, and data freshness explicit before rendering. That gives the UI library less to guess about, and gives the rest of the application rules that can be tested without opening a calendar.

articles.title: My OSS Projects: Codegen
articles.description: This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or...
articles.body_html:
This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or helped to grow – with the back story, what they do well, where they struggle, and what's next. Previous parts: AngleSharp, MAGES, Piral, Electron.NET, Netpack, Picard.js and dets.

And here we are: the last article of the series. Fittingly, it is about a project that is – in the best sense – small, boring and everywhere in my own toolchains: Codegen.

If you read the Piral article, you have already met it in passing. Today it gets the stage for itself.

What is Codegen?

A .codegen file is a Node.js module that writes another module.

That's the whole idea. You export a function. The function returns a string. The string is the module that your bundler continues to work with. In other words: you can program how a file looks to your application, using the full power of Node.js at build time.

// info.codegen
const { name, version } = require('../package.json');

module.exports = function () {
  return `
    export const name = ${JSON.stringify(name)};
    export const version = ${JSON.stringify(version)};
  `;
};

// app.ts
import { name, version } from './info.codegen';

console.log(`${name}@${version}`);

Your application never sees the require, the package.json, or the function. It sees two consts – the rest happened while bundling. If you like fancy words: this is metaprogramming. The program in the .codegen file describes what the module looks like from the outside.

How it came to be

The idea dates back to the very beginning of Piral. Back then, Piral used Parcel as its default bundler (as opposed to Webpack v5 today). A micro frontend framework needs to bend the bundler a bit: aliases, shared dependencies, externals, and a bunch of other things that you do not want to explain to every user in a bundler-specific way.

We looked at a couple of options and found that the best one is a custom format that controls all of this: the .codegen file. By referencing Piral you would indirectly reference a .codegen file, which is then picked up by the bundler. The user never has to know. They just npm install and go.

From there it grew a life of its own. I wrote about it in 2022 – Getting Bundling Superpowers Using Codegen – and since then, the family of plugins has grown to cover pretty much every bundler I come across.

How does it work?

The mechanism is the same everywhere:

  1. Your code imports a .codegen file.
  2. The bundler plugin recognizes the extension and, instead of loading the file as-is, evaluates it in Node.js.
  3. The exported function is called. It can be synchronous or async – so reading files and calling APIs is fair game.
  4. The returned string becomes the source of the module. From here on, the bundler treats it like any other module: it can contain imports, be TypeScript-ish or JSX-ish depending on your pipeline, be tree-shaken, and so on.

The function is called with a little context as this:

Member What it is
this.name The file that is being evaluated.
this.options Options of the build, e.g. outDir and rootDir.
this.addDependency(file) Tell the bundler: if this file changes, re-run the generator. (Crucial for watch mode.)

(That's why you should use function () {} and not an arrow function if you need the context.)

Under the hood, the plugins share one small library, codegen-lib, which loads the module (CommonJS by default; files named *.mjs.codegen, *.esm.codegen, *.module.codegen or *.m.codegen are loaded as ES modules), calls the function, and normalizes the result. Each plugin is only a thin layer that connects the library to a bundler's hooks: onLoad in esbuild, resolveId plus load in Vite, a loader in Webpack, a transformer in Parcel v2.

The real superpower: staying bundler-agnostic

When I explain .codegen to people, they often ask: "Why not just use a plugin for X / a config option for Y?"

The answer is: because you want to do something with the bundler without writing it for a bundler.

Say you build an app for the web and for mobile. The web build should use localStorage and fetch; the mobile build should use native storage and native HTTP. In bundler land you'd reach for aliases, define plugins, conditional exports, or some bundler-specific magic – and rewrite it all if you ever switch bundlers.

With codegen you just write what you mean:

// platform.codegen
module.exports = function () {
  const target = process.env.TARGET || 'web';
  return `export * from './platform.${target}';`;
};

// anywhere in the app
import { storage, http } from './platform.codegen';

The decision can be driven by an environment variable (as above), a special file, a call to a license server, the phase of the moon – whatever you want. It's just Node.js. And because the contract is "return a string", the same file works in Webpack, Parcel, Vite, esbuild, Rollup – and Netpack.

More examples

The nice thing about "it's just code" is that the possibilities are endless. Here are some that I find useful.

1. Build information

Stamp your app with the version, the commit and the build time – and do the computations while bundling instead of in the browser:

// build-info.codegen
const { execSync } = require('child_process');
const { name, version } = require('../package.json');

module.exports = function () {
  const commit = execSync('git rev-parse --short HEAD').toString().trim();
  const [major, minor, patch] = version.split('-')[0].split('.').map(Number);

  return `
    export const name = ${JSON.stringify(name)};
    export const version = ${JSON.stringify(version)};
    export const packageId = ${JSON.stringify(`${name}@${version}`)};
    export const major = ${major};
    export const minor = ${minor};
    export const patch = ${patch};
    export const isPrerelease = ${version.includes('-')};
    export const commit = ${JSON.stringify(commit)};
    export const builtAt = ${JSON.stringify(new Date().toISOString())};
  `;
};

import { packageId, major, isPrerelease } from './build-info.codegen';

A fair question: "Can't I just import { version } from '../package.json'?" You can – and that is a good option for the simple case. Many bundlers (Webpack, Rollup, Vite, esbuild, …) tree-shake JSON files, so if you use the fields as named exports, you don't get the full package.json in your bundle either. (Importing the file as a default object is a different story: you usually get all of it.)

So where is the difference? Codegen works on a finer granularity and allows a lot more:

  • Compile-time computation instead of runtime computation. Splitting the version into major, minor and patch, building the packageId, or checking for a pre-release is work you'd otherwise do in every user's browser, on every start. Here, the result is baked into the bundle as literals.
  • Literals unlock optimizations. The values are plain consts with literal values, so the bundler and the minifier see them as constants: they can be inlined at the use site, and if (isPrerelease) { … } can be removed entirely when the flag is false. With a runtime computation, that is impossible – the bundler can't know the result.
  • Unused exports still disappear. Just like with JSON, named exports that nobody imports are tree-shaken away. You can generate a rich module with ten fields and pay only for the ones you use.
  • Not limited to files. The commit hash comes from git, the build time from the clock. Neither lives in any file a bundler could import.

Tree shaking, in a nutshell: the bundler looks at which exports are actually used and drops the rest. It works best when a module is "static" – plain export const declarations with no side effects. And that's exactly what a good codegen file generates: static code, with all the dynamic parts resolved before the bundler even starts looking.

2. Feature flags that really disappear 

// flags.codegen
module.exports = function () {
  return `
    export const beta = ${process.env.BETA === '1'};
    export const telemetry = ${process.env.TELEMETRY !== '0'};
  `;
};

import { beta } from './flags.codegen';

if (beta) {
  // this block can be removed by the minifier when beta is false
}

Since the flags are plain consts with literal values, dead code elimination does its job. The flags don't exist at runtime, they were decided at build time.

3. Languages from a folder – with lazy loading

Add a de.json to your locales folder, and it shows up in the app. No registry to maintain:

// languages.codegen
const { readdirSync } = require('fs');
const { join, basename } = require('path');

module.exports = function () {
  const dir = join(__dirname, 'locales');
  const languages = readdirSync(dir)
    .filter((file) => file.endsWith('.json'))
    .map((file) => basename(file, '.json'));

  languages.forEach((lang) => this.addDependency(join(dir, `${lang}.json`)));

  const loaders = languages
    .map((lang) => `  ${JSON.stringify(lang)}: () => import(${JSON.stringify(`./locales/${lang}.json`)})`)
    .join(',\n');

  return `
    export const languages = ${JSON.stringify(languages)};
    export const load = {
${loaders}
    };
  `;
};

Each language becomes its own chunk, loaded only when somebody asks for it: const messages = await load['de'](). Note the addDependency: in watch mode, editing a locale file re-runs the generator.

4. File-system routing

Everybody loves the "every file in pages/ is a route" convention. With codegen you don't need a meta framework for it:

// routes.codegen
const { readdirSync } = require('fs');
const { join, relative, parse } = require('path');

function walk(dir) {
  return readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true }).flatMap((entry) =>
    entry.isDirectory() ? walk(join(dir, entry.name)) : [join(dir, entry.name)],
  );
}

module.exports = function () {
  const root = join(__dirname, 'pages');
  const entries = walk(root)
    .filter((file) => file.endsWith('.tsx'))
    .map((file) => {
      const rel = relative(root, file).split('\\').join('/');
      const { dir, name } = parse(rel);
      const path = '/' + (name === 'index' ? dir : [dir, name].filter(Boolean).join('/'));
      return `  { path: ${JSON.stringify(path)}, component: lazy(() => import(${JSON.stringify(`./pages/${rel}`)})) }`;
    });

  return `
    import { lazy } from 'react';
    export const routes = [
${entries.join(',\n')}
    ];
  `;
};

pages/index.tsx becomes /, pages/about/index.tsx becomes /about, pages/blog.tsx becomes /blog – each lazily loaded. (This is a simplified version of what I showed in the old article; dynamic segments like [id] are left as an exercise for the reader.)

5. Shared dependencies, à la Piral

This is the kind of thing that started it all. Say you want a module that lists the dependencies an app shell shares with its plugins:

// shared.codegen
const { dependencies } = require('../package.json');

const shared = ['react', 'react-dom', 'react-router-dom'].filter((name) => name in dependencies);

module.exports = function () {
  const entries = shared.map((name) => `  ${JSON.stringify(name)}: () => import(${JSON.stringify(name)})`);

  return `export const shared = {\n${entries.join(',\n')}\n};`;
};

(This is an illustration of the principle, not what Piral ships.) The list is derived from the package.json, so nobody has to maintain it by hand, and the bundler sees real import() calls, so everything gets split and resolved properly.

6. Generating a client from a schema – at build time

Because the function can be async, you can fetch things while bundling:

// api.codegen
module.exports = async function () {
  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/openapi.json');
  const spec = await response.json();

  const operations = Object.entries(spec.paths).flatMap(([path, methods]) =>
    Object.entries(methods).map(([method, op]) => ({ id: op.operationId, method: method.toUpperCase(), path })),
  );

  const functions = operations.map(
    ({ id, method, path }) =>
      `export const ${id} = (init) => fetch(${JSON.stringify(path)}, { method: ${JSON.stringify(method)}, ...init });`,
  );

  return functions.join('\n');
};

The result is a module with one function per operation, always in sync with the API as of the build. (Is that a good idea for your CI? Depends on your network. Which brings us to the caveats…)

7. A media library

One of the classics from the old article: take a folder of images and make them importable by name:

// media.codegen
const { readdirSync } = require('fs');
const { join, parse } = require('path');

module.exports = function () {
  const files = readdirSync(join(__dirname, 'avatars'));
  const imports = files.map((file, i) => `import _${i} from ${JSON.stringify(`./avatars/${file}`)};`);
  const entries = files.map((file, i) => `  ${JSON.stringify(parse(file).name)}: _${i}`);

  return `${imports.join('\n')}\nexport const images = {\n${entries.join(',\n')}\n};`;
};

Codegen in the wild

Piral

Piral is where it all started, and it is still a main consumer: referencing Piral means (indirectly) referencing .codegen files that the bundler plugin picks up. They handle aliases, shared dependencies and the other things a micro frontend needs from its bundler – on Parcel back then, on Webpack v5 today.

Piral.Blazor

For Piral.Blazor, codegen files are used to take a Blazor-powered pilet from the .NET world and bring it into the same format we already know and appreciate in the JS world. From the outside, it looks just like any other pilet.

Netpack

In Netpack, .codegen support lives behind the opt-in Node bridge. Netpack itself is a native .NET application – so, to evaluate a .codegen module, it makes an IPC call to Node.js, which evaluates the module and hands the resulting string back. The string then joins the bundling process like in any other bundler. (If you don't use .codegen, you don't need Node.js for the build. If you do: yes, a .NET bundler calls Node. I know.)

The plugin family

All plugins live in one repository: FlorianRappl/codegen-js. Here is the family:

Bundler Package
Webpack 4 / 5 parcel-codegen-loader
Parcel v1 (the original) parcel-plugin-codegen
Parcel v2 parcel-transformer-codegen
esbuild esbuild-codegen-plugin
Vite vite-plugin-codegen
Rollup rollup-plugin-codegen
Bun bun-codegen-loader
Netpack built in (via the Node bridge)

For Rspack you can use the Webpack loader – the setup is the same.

(Yes, the Webpack loader is called parcel-codegen-loader. History. The first plugin was for Parcel, and renaming things on npm is a special kind of pain.)

Setting it up

Pick your bundler; the setup is a one-time thing.

Webpack (rule with the loader):

module.exports = {
  module: {
    rules: [
      {
        test: /\.codegen$/i,
        use: [{ loader: 'parcel-codegen-loader' }],
      },
    ],
  },
};

Parcel v2 (.parcelrc):

{
  "extends": "@parcel/config-default",
  "transformers": {
    "*.codegen": ["parcel-transformer-codegen"]
  }
}

Vite and Rollup (plugin):

import codegen from 'vite-plugin-codegen'; // or 'rollup-plugin-codegen'

export default {
  plugins: [codegen()],
};

esbuild:

import { build } from 'esbuild';
import { codegenPlugin } from 'esbuild-codegen-plugin';

await build({
  // ...
  plugins: [codegenPlugin()],
});

From there, import x from './thing.codegen' just works.

The numbers

Not huge, not tiny: in the week from 25 June to 1 July 2026, the Webpack loader saw about 8,800 downloads, the Vite plugin about 3,800, the esbuild plugin ~200, Parcel v1 ~330, Rollup ~70 and Parcel v2 ~30. Each bundler has its own crowd, and Webpack's is the biggest.

A bit of history

The repository was consolidated at the end of 2024. Version 2.0.0 (26 December 2024) brought all packages together in one monorepo, split the core logic into codegen-lib, and added ESM output to the packages. 2.1.0 (same day) fixed a problem in the Webpack loader, introduced the Bun loader and limited the Parcel v1 plugin to CommonJS. There is also an official VS Code extension (florianrappl.vscode-codegen) that treats *.codegen as JavaScript and ships snippets for new files.

The practical side

TypeScript

TypeScript has no idea what a .codegen import contains. Put a declaration file next to it:

// info.codegen.d.ts
export const name: string;
export const version: string;

Testing

Your unit-test runner isn't a bundler, so it doesn't know .codegen either – unless it is built on one. There are three approaches: mock the import (jest.mock / vi.mock, or a small .js stand-in), add a transformer that evaluates the codegen files, or – if your runner is based on a bundler – use the plugin for it.

Jest has no bundler underneath, so you add a transform entry:

transform: {
  '^.+\\.codegen$': resolve(__dirname, 'codegen.js'),
},

(See the old article for a transformer implementation; Jest needs a synchronous one.)

Vitest is built on Vite and reuses its configuration and plugins. So there is nothing to write: if you already use vite-plugin-codegen for your app, the same plugin works in your tests. If you don't have a Vite config yet, add one for Vitest:

// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import codegen from 'vite-plugin-codegen';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [codegen()],
  test: {
    // your usual Vitest options
  },
});

Now import { version } from './build-info.codegen' in a test runs the real generator, just like in the build. And if you'd rather have a fixed result in a test, vi.mock('./build-info.codegen', () => ({ version: '1.0.0' })) does the job.

Debugging

Remember: the generated module is what gets bundled. If something looks wrong, console.log the string your function returns. It's the single best debugging technique for codegen.

Where Codegen shines

  • Bundler-agnostic. One mechanism, many bundlers. Switch bundlers, keep your codegen files.
  • No new language. It's Node.js. Everyone already knows how to read files, call fetch or look at process.env.
  • Maximum control. Build-time decisions become plain constants; generated imports become normal chunks.
  • Small. The plugins are tiny wrappers around one shared library.
  • Great for conventions. "Every file in this folder is X" becomes a ten-line generator instead of a manual registry.

Where it struggles

Let's be honest:

  • It runs arbitrary code at build time. A .codegen file has full Node.js access: it can read secrets, call the network, and run commands. Treat these files like build scripts, not like app code – because that's what they are.
  • No parameters. A .codegen file can't take arguments from the importer. The workarounds are generating several modules, or exporting many named values from one and letting tree shaking remove the unused ones. Dynamic import() can't take parameters either, so lazy-loading recipes generate loadX functions per file.
  • It's not cached. Every load re-runs the generator. Expensive generators (network!) make for slow builds, so keep them lean or do the caching yourself.
  • CommonJS first. CJS is the default; ES module generators are possible via the .esm.codegen-style names, but the ESM loader only rewrites simple import x from './y' statements. If you stay on the common path, it's fine; if you get fancy, you'll find the edge.
  • Debugging is indirect. The code you ran is not the code you ship – by design, and sometimes annoying.
  • Editor support is minimal. The VS Code extension treats the files as JavaScript and ships snippets; that's about it.
  • Tests. The repository doesn't contain a dedicated test suite; the plugins are small, but be aware of it.

What's next

Honestly: not much has to happen. It's one of the "finished" kind of projects – a tiny mechanism that does its job. The most visible movement lately has been breadth: new bundlers keep appearing (the Bun loader was the newest addition in 2.1.0). (Rspack doesn't even need its own plugin – the Webpack loader works there.) When a new bundler gets traction, adding another thin wrapper around codegen-lib is an afternoon.

If you have an idea for a codegen recipe that deserves to be in the docs – or a bundler that deserves a plugin – open an issue or a pull request against the develop branch.

Links

  • 💻 GitHub: FlorianRappl/codegen-js
  • 📝 The original article: Getting Bundling Superpowers Using Codegen
  • 🧩 VS Code: florianrappl.vscode-codegen

That's a wrap

This was the last article of the series. Thanks for reading all the way through! Here are all the parts, in case you missed one:

  1. AngleSharp – the .NET HTML parser that started it all.
  2. MAGES – a parser and interpreter for mathematical expressions.
  3. Piral – the micro frontend framework.
  4. Electron.NET – .NET meets Electron.
  5. Netpack – a native bundler for the .NET world.
  6. Picard.js – a lightweight micro frontend orchestrator.
  7. dets – a TypeScript declaration file bundler.
  8. Codegen – metaprogramming for your bundler (you are here).

If something in the series resonated with you: try the projects, open an issue, send a pull request, or just say hi. Open source lives from the people who use it.

articles.body_html:
Description: Python security, screen capture, spring physics, HiDPI and PyInstaller .exe gotchas. 7 tests from shipping 3 no-telemetry Python apps for Windows (ATLOCK, ASNIPP, APIC).

Most Python developers can write a for loop, a Flask route and a pandas one-liner.

Python experts know what happens before line 1 runs, what Python can't do, and what breaks the moment your script leaves your laptop.

I found out which one I was while building three Windows desktop apps in pure Python: ATLOCK (a security suite), ASNIPP (a screenshot and screen recorder) and APIC (an image toolkit). No ads, no analytics SDKs, no bloat. Every test below is a real bug or design decision from one of them.

Score yourself honestly. 👇

Test 1: Do you know that import order can be a security decision? (ATLOCK)

Quick: what does import ctypes have to do with security?

On Windows, a DLL imported later can be loaded from the current directory. That is how DLL planting attacks work. The fix has to run before the other imports:

import sys, ctypes

if sys.platform == "win32":
    k32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
    k32.SetDllDirectoryW.argtypes = [ctypes.c_wchar_p]
    k32.SetDllDirectoryW("")                      # drop the CWD from the DLL search path
    k32.SetDefaultDllDirectories.argtypes = [ctypes.c_uint32]
    k32.SetDefaultDllDirectories(0x1000)          # LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS

# only NOW import the heavy stuff
import cryptography, argon2

Developer: puts imports in alphabetical order.
Expert: knows import order is a runtime security boundary.

This is the very first thing that runs in ATLOCK, my pure-Python security suite.

Test 2: Can your screen recorder avoid recording itself? (ASNIPP)

I built a screen recorder with a floating control bar. First recording: the bar showed up in the video. 🤦

You don't need to hide and show windows. One Win32 call, straight from Python, does it:

import ctypes

def exclude_from_capture(widget):
    hwnd = int(widget.winId())
    # 0x11 = WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE (Windows 10 2004+)
    ctypes.windll.user32.SetWindowDisplayAffinity(hwnd, 0x11)

The window stays visible to you and is invisible to every screen capture. That is how ASNIPP keeps its own toolbars, drawing overlay and recording border out of your videos.

Developer: crops the bar out in post.
Expert: knows ctypes gives Python the whole Windows API.

Test 3: Can your app decide what you meant, without asking? (APIC)

Good desktop software removes clicks. In APIC, my image toolkit, the rule is simple:

  • Drop one image → open it in the editor.
  • Drop many → open the batch converter. 
def on_files(self, paths: list[str]):
    if not paths:
        paths, _ = QFileDialog.getOpenFileNames(
            self, "Open Image(s)", "",
            "Images (*.png *.jpg *.jpeg *.webp *.bmp *.tiff *.gif *.ico *.heic *.avif)")
    if len(paths) == 1:
        self.open_in_edit(paths[0])
    elif paths:
        self.open_in_convert(paths)

def dropEvent(self, event):
    self.on_files([u.toLocalFile() for u in event.mimeData().urls()])

The home screen, the file dialog and drag-and-drop all go through one function. Add a new entry point and you add zero logic.

Developer: writes three code paths.
Expert: writes one funnel and lets every input flow into it. The UI is split into one module per mode (edit, convert, compress, search), and main.py only wires them together.

Test 4: Do you know the difference between "encrypted" and "encrypted correctly"? (ATLOCK)

Developer: AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB) and done.

Expert checklist:

  • AEAD, not just encryption: AES-256-GCM authenticates every chunk.
  • Slow KDF for passwords: Argon2id, not a bare SHA-256.
  • Never reuse a nonce with the same key.
  • Bind the header with AAD so metadata can't be swapped. 
import os
from argon2.low_level import hash_secret_raw, Type
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

def seal(password: bytes, data: bytes) -> bytes:
    salt = os.urandom(16)
    key = hash_secret_raw(password, salt, time_cost=3, memory_cost=64 * 1024,
                          parallelism=4, hash_len=32, type=Type.ID)
    nonce = os.urandom(12)
    ct = AESGCM(key).encrypt(nonce, data, associated_data=b"v1")
    return salt + nonce + ct

(Simplified. ATLOCK's real container format also does chunking, key commitment and versioning.)

Test 5: Can you make a Qt animation feel alive with 6 lines of math? (ASNIPP)

ASNIPP's capture bar is a "Dynamic Island" that bounces open. Qt's built-in easing curves felt stiff, so I wrote a damped spring and plugged it into QEasingCurve:

import math
from PyQt6.QtCore import QEasingCurve

def spring(zeta, omega):
    wd = omega * math.sqrt(max(1e-6, 1 - zeta * zeta)) if zeta < 1 else 0.0
    def f(t):
        if t <= 0: return 0.0
        if t >= 1: return 1.0
        if zeta < 1:    # under-damped: overshoots, then settles (the bounce)
            return 1 - math.exp(-zeta * omega * t) * (math.cos(wd * t) + (zeta * omega / wd) * math.sin(wd * t))
        return 1 - math.exp(-omega * t) * (1 + omega * t)   # critically damped: no overshoot
    return f

BOUNCY = spring(0.66, 11.0)   # keep it at MODULE level (see below)

curve = QEasingCurve(QEasingCurve.Type.Linear)
curve.setCustomType(BOUNCY)

The trap: if the function is a temporary object, Python garbage-collects it while Qt still holds a pointer, and you get random crashes. Keep custom callables alive at module level. Only people who've been bitten know this one.

Test 6: Does your app look sharp on a 4K laptop with 150% scaling? (APIC)

Most Python GUI apps look blurry or oddly sized on modern displays. In Qt 6 the fix is one policy before you create the app:

from PyQt6.QtWidgets import QApplication
from PyQt6.QtCore import Qt

QApplication.setHighDpiScaleFactorRoundingPolicy(
    Qt.HighDpiScaleFactorRoundingPolicy.PassThrough)   # no rounding: 125%/150% stay crisp

app = QApplication(sys.argv)
app.setApplicationName("APIC")
app.setOrganizationName("Akhouri Systems")

PassThrough keeps fractional scales like 125% and 150% exact instead of snapping to 100% or 200%. Add one try/except AttributeError for older Qt builds, and your app looks native everywhere.

Developer: tests on their own monitor.
Expert: tests at 100%, 125%, 150% and 200%.

Test 7: Can you explain why Python can't truly erase a password from memory? (ATLOCK) 

password = "hunter2"
password = None   # is it gone? 🙂

No. Python str and bytes are immutable, and the interpreter is free to copy them. The best you can do is keep secrets in a mutable bytearray and wipe it explicitly:

buf = bytearray(b"hunter2")
# ... use it ...
for i in range(len(buf)):
    buf[i] = 0

An honest Python security tool says this out loud instead of promising magic. ATLOCK's source header lists what it can't do: memory wiping is best-effort, SSD shredding can't be guaranteed, and a same-user attacker can modify the script. Python experts document their limits.

Bonus: "Why does it work in VS Code and silently do nothing as a .exe?"

All three of my apps ship as Python compiled with PyInstaller (--onefile --windowed). It cost me an evening before I learned this: in a windowed build, sys.stdout and sys.stderr are None. Any print(), logging call or library traceback can fail silently, and your app "just doesn't open."

import sys, os

for name in ("stdout", "stderr"):
    if getattr(sys, name, None) is None:
        setattr(sys, name, open(os.devnull, "w", encoding="utf-8"))

# and show errors somewhere a human can see them:
import ctypes
ctypes.windll.user32.MessageBoxW(None, "Startup failed: ...", "App error", 0x10)

Try the code yourself

I'm the developer behind all of this, and the three apps are the proof that it works outside tutorials. They're built by Akhouri Systems, each is pure Python packaged as an .exe in a zip, with no ads and no analytics. The only network features are the ones you trigger yourself (for example ATLOCK's optional breach check, which sends only a 5-character hash prefix).

articles.title: How I finally understood the Dependency Inversion Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Last stop. We made it to the D: the Dependency Inversion Principle.  This one is...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Last stop. We made it to the D: the Dependency Inversion Principle.

This one is special because the other four kind of lead here. SRP gave us small classes. OCP taught us to add instead of edit. LSP and ISP gave us honest, tiny interfaces. DIP is where we decide who points at whom.

Buckle up, it's the one that changes how your main.ts looks forever.

The What

The definition has two parts:

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions.

Four sentences that use "depend" five times. Cool cool cool.

Plain version: your business logic should not import your database driver. The important stuff (orders, invoices, rules) should sit at the top and know nothing about the plumbing (Postgres, Stripe, the file system). The plumbing should plug into the business logic, not the other way around.

Let's build an order checkout and watch the arrows flip.

The How

Here is OrderService, the "high-level" part of our store. It's the thing that knows what placing an order means:

// src/order-service.ts
import { PostgresOrderRepository } from './postgres-order-repository.js'
import { StripeClient } from './stripe-client.js'

export class OrderService {
  private readonly orders = new PostgresOrderRepository('postgres://localhost/shop')
  private readonly stripe = new StripeClient(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!)

  async placeOrder(customerId: string, total: number) {
    await this.stripe.charge(customerId, total)
    const id = await this.orders.insert({ customerId, total })
    console.log(`🧾 order ${id} placed`)
    return id
  }
}

The two "low-level" pieces:

// src/postgres-order-repository.ts
export class PostgresOrderRepository {
  constructor(private readonly url: string) {}

  async insert(order: { customerId: string; total: number }) {
    console.log(`🐘 INSERT INTO orders ... (${this.url})`)
    return 'ord_123'
  }
}

// src/stripe-client.ts
export class StripeClient {
  constructor(private readonly apiKey: string) {}

  async charge(customerId: string, amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 stripe charged ${customerId} $${amount}`)
  }
}

And main:

// src/main.ts
import { OrderService } from './order-service.js'

await new OrderService().placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

Run it, it works, everyone goes home. 🏠

Now draw the arrows. Who imports whom?

OrderService  ──▶  PostgresOrderRepository
OrderService  ──▶  StripeClient

The most important class in the app depends on the two most replaceable classes in the app. That's upside down. And here's how you feel it:

  • Want to write a test for placeOrder()? Congratulations, your test now needs a running Postgres and a Stripe API key. For a function with two lines of logic.
  • Marketing wants a free-trial checkout with no payment? You're going to put an if inside OrderService to skip Stripe. Then another for the sandbox. Then...
  • The database team migrates to MySQL? Open OrderService, the one file that should never care.
  • Running it locally charges a real card if STRIPE_KEY is a real key. Ask me how I know. 😬

The service news its own dependencies, so it is welded to them. Let's cut the welds.

Step 1: the high-level module describes what it needs

OrderService needs two things: somewhere to put orders, and something that can take money. It should describe those in its own words, not in Postgres or Stripe words:

// src/order-service.ts
export interface NewOrder {
  customerId: string
  total: number
}

export interface OrderRepository {
  insert(order: NewOrder): Promise<string>
}

export interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(customerId: string, amount: number): Promise<void>
}

export class OrderService {
  constructor(
    private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    private readonly payments: PaymentGateway,
  ) {}

  async placeOrder(customerId: string, total: number) {
    await this.payments.charge(customerId, total)
    const id = await this.orders.insert({ customerId, total })
    console.log(`🧾 order ${id} placed`)
    return id
  }
}

Two things to notice:

  1. The interfaces live next to the service, because the service owns them. It says "this is what I need". That's the "abstractions belong to the high level" part.
  2. The dependencies come in through the constructor. The service doesn't build them anymore. That's the "dependency injection" part, which is the everyday tool we use to follow DIP.

Step 2: the details plug in 

// src/postgres-order-repository.ts
import type { OrderRepository, NewOrder } from './order-service.js'

export class PostgresOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  constructor(private readonly url: string) {}

  async insert(order: NewOrder) {
    console.log(`🐘 INSERT INTO orders ... (${this.url})`)
    return 'ord_123'
  }
}

// src/stripe-payment-gateway.ts
import type { PaymentGateway } from './order-service.js'

export class StripePaymentGateway implements PaymentGateway {
  constructor(private readonly apiKey: string) {}

  async charge(customerId: string, amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 stripe charged ${customerId} $${amount}`)
  }
}

Look at the imports now. The Postgres class imports from order-service.ts. The arrow flipped:

PostgresOrderRepository  ──▶  OrderRepository (owned by OrderService)
StripePaymentGateway     ──▶  PaymentGateway  (owned by OrderService)

The plumbing points at the business logic. That's the "inversion".

Step 3: main.ts becomes the only place that knows everything 

// src/main.ts
import { OrderService } from './order-service.js'
import { PostgresOrderRepository } from './postgres-order-repository.js'
import { StripePaymentGateway } from './stripe-payment-gateway.js'

const service = new OrderService(
  new PostgresOrderRepository('postgres://localhost/shop'),
  new StripePaymentGateway(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!),
)

await service.placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

Same output as before. But now the big one: let's write that test.

Step 4: the test that used to be impossible 

// src/order-service.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest'
import { OrderService, type OrderRepository, type PaymentGateway } from './order-service.js'

class InMemoryOrders implements OrderRepository {
  saved: unknown[] = []
  async insert(order: unknown) {
    this.saved.push(order)
    return 'ord_test'
  }
}

class FakePayments implements PaymentGateway {
  charged: number[] = []
  async charge(_customerId: string, amount: number) {
    this.charged.push(amount)
  }
}

test('placing an order charges and saves it', async () => {
  const orders = new InMemoryOrders()
  const payments = new FakePayments()
  const service = new OrderService(orders, payments)

  const id = await service.placeOrder('cus_42', 99)

  expect(id).toBe('ord_test')
  expect(payments.charged).toEqual([99])
  expect(orders.saved).toHaveLength(1)
})

No Postgres. No Stripe. No mocking library. Two tiny classes that implement the interfaces OrderService asked for, and a test that runs in a millisecond.

And the free-trial checkout from earlier? new OrderService(repo, new NoChargeGateway()). Zero ifs inside the service.

The Why

Let's land this plane:

  • Business logic is the stable part; vendors are the volatile part. Stable code should never import volatile code. DIP is just that sentence turned into a rule.
  • Interfaces belong to the consumer. OrderService wrote PaymentGateway in its own vocabulary. Stripe adapted to it, not the other way around. When you swap Stripe for something else, the interface doesn't move.
  • Construction happens at the edge. main.ts (or your DI container, or your framework's wiring) is the only place that says new PostgresOrderRepository(...). Everything inside is handed what it needs.
  • Testing is a side effect, not a goal. We didn't "design for testability". We pointed the arrows the right way and the tests became easy on their own.

If you read my loosely coupled modules post, this should feel familiar. Same move, now with a name and a letter.

The Goodbye

And that's SOLID, all five letters, five tiny projects, five things we broke on purpose. If I had to compress the series into one line:

Small honest pieces, pointed at abstractions, glued together at the front door.

Thanks for riding along. Now go find a new keyword inside a service class and ask it why it's there. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: Why Changing an Agent Harness Breaks Frozen Models
articles.description: Benchmarking coding agent harnesses with a frozen model conflates interface capabilities with policy mismatch.
articles.body_html:
Whenever a team releases a new agent harness, the evaluation script looks the same. You take a popular checkpoint, wire it up to the new prompt templates, tool signatures, and system loop, and measure task resolution against an older setup.

If the success rate drops, the team concludes the new harness is worse.

A new paper from Jian Mu, Ruibo Shen, and Yao Shu at HKUST (Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces, arXiv:2610.37255) shows why this standard comparison is broken. Under KL-regularized control, an optimal policy inherits the structural preferences of the exact harness it was post-trained on. When you evaluate harnesses using a frozen model, you are not testing which harness offers a better ceiling. You are measuring the combination of that ceiling and the mismatch penalty incurred by a policy trained on a different setup.

The paper formalizes deployed return as two distinct terms:

Return = Ceiling(Harness) - Mismatch(Policy, Harness)

The ceiling represents the maximum return possible under that harness. The mismatch represents the return lost because the current model makes suboptimal decisions under those specific interface mechanics.

Weight training moves mismatch. Swapping the harness moves both terms simultaneously.

The sensitivity of frozen policies

When an agent undergoes post-training under a specific harness, its log odds align with that harness's action distribution. The model learns to expect observations in a precise order, predicts tool responses shaped by particular wrappers, and paces its reasoning around a concrete turn loop.

The authors tested this sensitivity on MiniWoB++. They took a trained policy that solved 85.0% of tasks, kept all task semantics identical, and simply reversed the order of the observation fields in the prompt.

Every optimal action remained completely valid and achievable. Yet the success rate of the frozen model collapsed from 85.0% to 19.2%.

If you treated that test as an interface comparison, you would conclude that field order destroyed the environment. In reality, the environment ceiling remained identical, while the policy mismatch exploded because the frozen weights expected the original token layout.

Conversely, the authors found that every harness rejected by a frozen-model comparison that actually raised the theoretical ceiling went on to outperform the original harness once the agent was trained under it. Measuring ceiling and mismatch beforehand accurately predicted those downstream gains.

Measuring coding harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite

To see how this plays out in production environments, the team evaluated five prominent coding agent setups on Terminal-Bench Lite: DeepAgents, Pi, DeepSeek Harness, Terminus-2, and mini-SWE-agent. They ran a frozen Qwen3.5-9B across all five harnesses and used GPT-5.6 Luna as a teacher stand-in to estimate the true ceiling.

The ranking of actual task accuracy matched the ranking produced by estimating the ceiling minus mismatch:

Harness Ranking on Terminal-Bench Lite:
1. DeepAgents      (High ceiling, controlled mismatch via runtime recovery)
2. Pi              (Interactive terminal steering, compact state representations)
3. DeepSeek Harness (Structured tool profiles, rigid parameter enforcement)
4. Terminus-2      (Tmux session tracking, heavy prompt overhead on small models)
5. mini-SWE-agent  (Minimalist shell loop, lower structural ceiling on complex tasks)

Looking at either metric in isolation failed to predict performance. Looking only at raw accuracy hid whether a harness was genuinely limited or whether Qwen3.5-9B was stumbling over unexpected tool schema definitions.

For instance, Terminus-2 uses tmux keystroke buffers and native summarizer subagents. That architecture offers high ceiling capabilities on long interactive debugging tasks, but imposes high mismatch on smaller local models that fail to track asynchronous terminal state without specific fine-tuning. Meanwhile, mini-SWE-agent has low mismatch because its single-shot bash runner matches standard base model pretraining, but its ceiling is lower when tasks require managing multi-step background processes.

Stop treating harnesses as plug-and-play skins

The immediate takeaway for anyone building agent harnesses is clear: stop benchmarking harness revisions against frozen base checkpoints and calling it an architectural verdict.

When you modify prompt scaffolding, rewrite tool JSON schemas, or change how subagents pass context back to the root, you alter the action space. If your evaluation run shows a 10% regression on a base checkpoint, that regression does not prove your new tool schema is bad. It often means your model spent its post-training budget learning the quirks of your old schema.

If you want to compare harnesses fairly, you have two real options. You either fine-tune checkpoints under each harness candidate to measure adapted return, or you estimate the harness ceiling using a stronger teacher model and evaluate mismatch explicitly.

Anything else is just testing how well a model memorized the flaws of your first prototype.
