articles.title: My Daemon Dropped 1,000 Records and Reported Success
articles.description: A soak test came back green. Chain intact, verify-store fine, p99 latency 0.36 ms. Then I counted the...
articles.body_html:
A soak test came back green. Chain intact, verify-store fine, p99 latency 0.36 ms. Then I counted the rows: 9,016 out of 10,000. About a thousand records had gone missing, and every caller had been told the write succeeded.

This is the kind of failure that a background thread holding a lock the hot path needs produces — and raising a buffer to "fix" it is the wrong first move.

Two threads, one lock

The agentwatch recorder daemon — one tool in agentic-suite, a suite of open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI agents — has two threads that matter.

Thread 1 — Accept (the hot path): accepts Unix socket connections from hooks, reads the message, normalizes it, appends it to the hash-chained store.

def _append(self, record):
    with self._lock:            # ← needs store._lock
        self.store.append(record)

Thread 2 — Sweeper (background verification): every 5 seconds, reloads the store from disk and re-verifies the entire hash chain. This is continuous verification — if someone tampers with the store file mid-session, the sweeper detects it and flips health to degraded.

def _sweep_loop(self):
    while not self._stop.wait(5.0):
        self.chain_status = self.store.refresh()   # ← the problem

Both threads need store._lock. And refresh() was greedy about it:

def refresh(self):
    with self._lock:
        self._entries = self._load()   # read the ENTIRE file from disk
        self._recount()
        return self.verify()           # recompute EVERY hash — O(n)

Reading the file and rehashing the chain, start to finish, with the lock held the whole time. At small scale this is invisible — and that's exactly why it survives into a soak test.

What that cost

At a thousand entries it's nothing. Eleven milliseconds. At five thousand, fifty-six. At ten thousand, about a hundred and sixteen. By the end of a 10k-send soak the store held around twenty thousand entries, and a single sweep took 242 milliseconds.

Here's what happens during those 242 ms:

  1. The sweeper acquires store._lock.
  2. It reads the entire store file from disk (_load()).
  3. It recomputes every hash in the chain (verify() — O(n)).
  4. Meanwhile, the accept thread tries to append(). It blocks on store._lock.
  5. New hook connections queue in the listen backlog (512 slots).
  6. At ~200 records/sec, ~48 appends queue during the 242 ms lock hold.
  7. If the backlog fills before the sweeper releases, send() connects time out (1 s timeout).
  8. send() returns False. The hook is fire-and-forget — the agent doesn't retry. The record is lost.

Over 100 seconds of soak, the sweeper runs 20 times (every 5 s). Each sweep blocks ~48 appends. 20 × 48 = 960 blocked appends. 9,036 of 10,000 delivered. 964 silently lost.

The agent doesn't know. send() returns False, but the hook is fire-and-forget — the agent ignores the return value. The daemon doesn't log the dropped sends. The store has 9,036 records instead of 10,000, and the only way to notice is to count.

The fix that wasn't a fix

The first diagnosis was wrong, and it cost two full test runs.

"The single-threaded accept path is the bottleneck." The listen backlog was 128, so it got raised:

# Before
server.listen(128)

# After
server.listen(512)

Result: 9,499/10,000 (95%). Better. Still dropping 500.

The first run before any backlog change was 9,016/10,000 (90%). Raising to 512 moved it to 9,499 (95%). The improvement was real but the problem was unchanged — more queue room just meant more sends waited longer before timing out. The drop rate went from 10% to 5%, but 500 records still vanished.

The diagnosis was "the accept path can't keep up." The actual problem was "the accept path is blocked." Those look the same from the outside — sends are being dropped — but the fix is completely different. The first says "make the accept path faster or give it more room." The second says "stop holding the lock it needs."

Because more backlog doesn't prevent drops — it delays them. The bottleneck was never queue capacity. It was the time append() spent blocked on the lock. More backlog means more sends queue before timing out, but they still time out if the sweeper holds the lock long enough.

tip: Raising a backlog, pool size, or buffer to "fix" a performance issue is usually a band-aid. If the bottleneck is lock-hold time, more queue room just delays the drops. Measure the lock-hold time before you touch the queue.

Two full suite runs went to a band-aid before the actual lock got measured.

The right fix: snapshot, then verify

Move the expensive work out of the critical section. Read and verify without the lock, then swap the in-memory reference under the lock — O(1):

def refresh(self):
    entries = self._load()                  # disk read — no lock
    status = self._verify_entries(entries)  # O(n) verify — no lock

    with self._lock:                        # O(1) reference swap
        if len(entries) >= len(self._entries):
            self._entries = entries
        self._recount()
    return status

The lock now covers a pointer assignment instead of 242 ms of work. The accept thread never blocks for more than microseconds.

tip: Never hold a lock the hot path needs while doing O(n) work. Snapshot under the lock, process outside it, swap the reference in O(1). The work doesn't get faster — the critical section gets 242 ms smaller.

Result: 10,000/10,000 delivered. p99 = 0.36 ms. verify-store green.

The second bug the fix introduced

The very next run after that change failed:

agentsec-agentwatch: chain broken at seq 815

Moving the read outside the lock introduced a race. The disk read (_load()) runs without the lock. While it's reading, append() may write new entries to the file. The disk read can complete before those writes land, producing a shorter entry list — 815 entries instead of 820.

If refresh() then replaces self._entries with this shorter list, the next append() computes seq = 815 + 1 = 816 and prev_hash = entries[815].hash. But entry 816 was already written to disk by the append() that happened during the disk read. Now there are two entries with seq 816 on disk. The chain is broken.

The fix is the length guard:

if len(entries) >= len(self._entries):   # never adopt a stale, shorter snapshot
    self._entries = entries

If the disk snapshot is shorter than what's in memory, keep memory. Verification still runs on the snapshot — and may detect tampering — but the in-memory state is not corrupted. The next sweep picks up whatever it missed.

This is the subtle cost of moving work outside a lock. When the lock protected both the read and the swap, the snapshot was always consistent with memory by construction. When the read happens unlocked, the snapshot can be stale — and "stale" means "shorter than reality" in an append-only store. The length guard turns a potential chain break into a benign missed sweep.

The scaling table

The total refresh() time is the same — the file read and verification still take O(n). What changed is what is locked:

Store entries refresh() total time Lock held for
1,000 11 ms ~0 ms (reference swap)
5,000 56 ms ~0 ms
10,000 116 ms ~0 ms
20,000 242 ms ~0 ms

The work didn't get faster. The critical section got 242 ms smaller.

What I keep repeating to myself

O(n) under a contended lock is a scaling cliff. It works at low n, fails at high n, and fails silently and load-dependently — invisible in unit tests, visible only under sustained load.

Silent data loss is worse than a crash. A crash is visible. A dropped record with a success response is a lie the operator can't see. At least a crash tells you something broke.

The symptom doesn't point at the cause. "Sends are being dropped" sends you to the network, the backlog, the accept loop. The real cause was lock contention in a background thread. Per-thread timing is what diagnoses it.

It's fixed in agentwatch v0.1.0, and the 10k soak is the regression test that keeps it fixed.

The question worth asking of your own system: what's the lock-hold time of your background work at 10× your current scale? If it hasn't been measured, it's probably the thing blocking the hot path.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.1.0 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools
  • Field test report (defect D-1, FT-28)
  • Soak evidence: FT-28/
  • Store: store.py

articles.title: Your agent can't use a tool it never finds
articles.description: An agent is asked to find GitHub issues and put a summary in a spreadsheet.  It finds three...
articles.body_html:
An agent is asked to find GitHub issues and put a summary in a spreadsheet.

It finds three issue-search tools. It can read tickets, inspect comments, and filter bugs. The spreadsheet tool exists too. It just never makes it into the agent's context.

Now the agent has to work with an incomplete menu. It might stop, ask for help, or try to finish with the wrong tools. Better reasoning alone won't put the missing capability back on that menu.

This is the trade-off behind on-demand tool discovery: you stop loading every tool definition into the prompt, but you take on a retrieval problem before tool selection can even begin.

The useful question isn't only "Did the model choose the right tool?"

It's "Was the right tool available to choose?"

The optimization is real

Loading every schema upfront gets expensive as an agent connects to more services. Definitions compete with the conversation, task data, and intermediate results for context.

Anthropic's advanced tool-use introduction describes deferring tool definitions until a model searches for them. In one illustrated setup, it reports roughly 77,000 tokens of initial context consumption with the traditional approach versus 8,700 with tool search. It also reports better results on its internal MCP evaluations.

Those are vendor-reported results for particular setups, not a promise that adding search will improve every agent. The same post says discovery adds a search step and is less useful for small, compact tool libraries whose tools are used frequently.

This isn't confined to one API. Spring AI's implementation supports semantic, keyword, and regex search over tool definitions. Its guide describes the same basic sequence:

  1. Keep a catalog of tools outside the model's initial context.
  2. Let the model search for a capability.
  3. Expand matching definitions into context.
  4. Let the model choose and call a tool.

That third step is where a new kind of failure can become invisible if you only inspect the final tool call.

Discovery and selection are different tests

Suppose the task needs two capabilities:

  • Search issues.
  • Append spreadsheet rows.

A discovery result containing five issue tools and no spreadsheet tool is incomplete, even if every returned tool is relevant to part of the request.

The Dynamic ReAct paper gives a closely related example: retrieval for a Twitter-to-Google-Sheets workflow returns a Twitter-only subset. Its proposed search-and-load design uses separate, focused queries for different operations instead of treating the whole request as one search query.

MCP-Zero addresses another limit of one-shot retrieval: later steps can require tools that weren't obvious from the original request. Its design lets an agent request more capabilities as the task develops.

These papers don't establish one universally best retriever. They do make a useful architectural point: finding tools is part of the workflow, not necessarily a one-time setup step.

An original conceptual diagram, not benchmark data.

A small test you can run without a model

You don't need to call an LLM to catch the most basic discovery regressions. Start with a few tasks and the capabilities each task requires.

The script below deliberately uses a weak lexical search over a tiny, invented catalog. It is a constructed example, not a measurement of MCP, embeddings, or any model. Its purpose is to show how a retrieval test can expose a missing capability before you evaluate agent behavior.

import re

CATALOG = {
    "issues.search": "search issue tickets bugs github project",
    "issues.read": "read issue ticket details github project",
    "issues.comments": "read issue ticket comments github project",
    "chat.search": "search team chat messages slack",
    "chat.thread": "read team chat message thread slack",
    "sheets.append": "append rows spreadsheet google sheets",
    "sheets.read": "read rows spreadsheet google sheets",
}

def terms(text):
    return set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower()))

def search(query, k=2):
    q = terms(query)
    ranked = sorted(
        CATALOG,
        key=lambda t: (-len(q & terms(CATALOG[t])), t),
    )
    return [t for t in ranked if q & terms(CATALOG[t])][:k]

task = (
    "Find github issue tickets and bugs in a project "
    "and log results to a spreadsheet"
)
required = {"issues.search", "sheets.append"}

whole_task = set(search(task))
split_task = set(search("search issue tickets")) | set(
    search("append rows spreadsheet")
)

print("Missing, whole task:", sorted(required - whole_task))
print("Missing, split task:", sorted(required - split_task))

Output:

Missing, whole task: ['sheets.append']
Missing, split task: []

The whole-task query is dominated by issue-related vocabulary. Both result slots go to issue tools. Separate queries recover the spreadsheet capability.

There's a cost: in this example the split queries return four unique candidates rather than two. This is not evidence that splitting is always better at an equal token budget. It shows why "we reduced the number of visible tools" is an incomplete success metric.

For a real evaluation, compare approaches at the same total schema-token budget, or report the extra cost alongside the coverage improvement. Use tasks your users actually ask, including their vocabulary, not only phrases copied from your tool descriptions.

Measure the part that failed

I would keep these measurements separate:

Discovery coverage. For each task, did the retrieved set include at least one valid tool for every required capability? Some capabilities have multiple valid implementations, so don't grade every task against one hard-coded tool name.

Selection correctness. Given a complete candidate set, did the agent choose an appropriate tool? A tool that is visible but ignored is a different problem from one that was never retrieved.

Argument and task correctness. Did the agent supply valid, appropriate arguments and complete the actual job? A perfect retrieval score doesn't establish either.

Cost. Track schema tokens, discovery calls, latency, and extra candidates. A high-coverage search that loads the entire catalog has given up much of the intended saving.

A useful trace records the discovery query, candidate IDs and ranks, definitions actually loaded, selected tool, and any later search. Keep sensitive arguments out of broadly shared logs.

Then an unsuccessful run has somewhere to point:

  • Required capability never surfaced: inspect retrieval, catalog freshness, or filtering.
  • Capability surfaced but wasn't loaded: inspect the search-to-load step.
  • Definition loaded but wrong tool chosen: inspect selection.
  • Correct tool chosen but task failed: inspect arguments, execution, and the result.

That is more actionable than putting every failure in a bucket called "the model got confused."

Don't mistake a partial catalog for poor search

Before tuning embeddings or rewriting descriptions, check that the catalog is complete for the caller.

The MCP tools specification supports pagination in tools/list. It also allows the returned tool set to vary with the authorization on the request. That means two failures can look identical from the model's seat:

  • The search index didn't contain the second page of tools.
  • The caller wasn't authorized to see those tools.

One needs a catalog fix. The other may be correct access control.

There's concrete community evidence for testing the first case: a May 2026 Claude Code issue reports tools beyond the first page disappearing after a list-change notification. The issue is closed as a duplicate. This is a historical report, not a claim that the bug remains in current releases.

It is still a useful regression test: paginate the catalog, change it, refresh it, and verify that tools from later pages remain discoverable.

A practical starting point

Keep a small set of frequently used tools directly available. Defer the rest when the catalog's size justifies the added machinery.

For compound tasks, allow more than one focused discovery query. If a later step reveals a new capability requirement, allow another search instead of forcing the agent to finish with its initial set.

Write tool descriptions around actual operations and objects. "Append rows to a spreadsheet" is easier to distinguish from "Read spreadsheet rows" than two descriptions that both say "Manage sheets." Include important constraints, but don't pack every description with unrelated keywords to win retrieval.

Give discovery a bounded failure path too: a reformulated query, a broader search, or a clear stop when the needed capability cannot be found. Don't quietly substitute a different action just because it ranked highly.

Finally, keep authorization at the execution boundary. A search result is a candidate, not permission. A tool's presence in context does not authorize a particular call, account, recipient, or side effect.

Tool search can make a large agent practical. But it changes the system you're testing.

Once capabilities are loaded on demand, the catalog and retriever become part of what the agent can do. Test whether the right capability reaches the model before asking whether the model used it well.

Sources

  • Anthropic: Introducing advanced tool use, November 24, 2025. Vendor examples and internal evaluations.
  • Spring AI: Dynamic tool discovery. Implementation guide; its preliminary benchmarks use a different setup from Anthropic's.
  • Dynamic ReAct. Research architecture and multi-service retrieval example.
  • MCP-Zero. Research on iterative capability discovery.
  • MCP tools specification, July 28, 2026. Catalog pagination and authorization-dependent availability.
  • Claude Code issue #59538. Historical community report, closed as a duplicate; not a current product verdict.

articles.title: Zeen: A New Systems Programming Language with a Comptime Engine
articles.description: Website: zeen-lang.tech Github: mealet/zeen  (Would appreciate if you'd leave a star on Github)      ...
articles.body_html:
Website: zeen-lang.tech
Github: mealet/zeen

(Would appreciate if you'd leave a star on Github)

What is Zeen

Zeen - a modern systems programming language designed for simplicity, safety, and predictable control over memory. It provides toolchains and compiler rules to operate data easily and drop it automatically after usage with move semantics to avoid any runtime overhead. The main idea is to create a tool to develop efficient software where most errors are caught at compile time.

Zeen took many design choices from Rust and Zig programming languages, which makes it more familiar for most developers. Besides that it introduces its own approach to ownership, memory management, and compile-time execution.

Development Tools

Besides compiler and set of libraries (core, std), Zeen has:

  • Editors plugins for VS Code and Neovim
  • Package manager Zora

Small Example 

fn print_this[T: Display](value: T) {
  @println("Yeah, I've printed this: {}", value);
}

fn main() {
  print_this(123);
  print_this("hello!");
}

Quick Start

  1. Install latest release following official guide from documentation.
  2. Create new project with Zora: 
zora new my_project
cd my_project
  1. Write code and run your binary package: 
zora run

New Comptime Engine

Last update v0.4.0 brought a lot of enhancements: frontend performance, new warnings system, new macros, fixed C ABI and Comptime Engine.

Zeen's comptime engine allows you to move some evaluations or constructions away from runtime to the compiler.

You can define and eval constants, create Comptime functions which can construct new types, export expressions and declarations, emit declarations into current scope, format print at the compile time and more. Here's some examples of it.

Simple constants and splicing:

comptime N = 16;
comptime SquaredN = N * N;

fn main() {
  @println("{} -> {}", N, SquaredN);
  @println("$(N) -> $(SquaredN)");
}

Advanced usage (declarations, type values and etc):

comptime fn pair_of(struct_name: comptime_str, a: zeen_type, b: zeen_type) zeen_decl {
  @zeen_decl(
    struct $(struct_name) {
      pub a: $(a),
      pub b: $(b),
    }
  )
}

comptime {
  @emit(pair_of("NumsPair", i32, f32));
}

fn main() {
  let pair = NumsPair { .a = 1, .b = 1.0 };
  @println("{} {}", pair.a, pair.b);
}

See more info and examples on changelog and comptime docs pages.

articles.title: # RepoGhost: Investigating GitHub Accounts Without Guessing 👻
articles.description: Every GitHub profile leaves a trail. The challenge is knowing what that trail actually tells...
articles.body_html:
Every GitHub profile leaves a trail. The challenge is knowing what that trail actually tells you.

I’m building RepoGhost, a project that investigates public GitHub accounts and repositories, surfaces useful evidence, and helps you ask questions about what it finds.

The idea is simple: instead of looking at a profile and making assumptions, investigate the projects behind it.

🔗 Live demo: https://repoghost.onrender.com

💻 GitHub repository: https://github.com/egbutaify2-ui/repoghost

Why I started building RepoGhost

A GitHub profile can contain dozens of repositories, different technologies, activity records, and projects with very different purposes.

But repository counts and star numbers alone don't tell the whole story.

I wanted to build something that could help answer practical questions:

  • What does this GitHub account or organization actually work on?
  • Which public repositories are relevant to a particular technology or role?
  • What technologies appear in its projects?
  • What can recent public activity tell us—and what can't we conclude from it?
  • Can I ask follow-up questions about an investigated account instead of starting from scratch?

That last question is especially important to me. I want RepoGhost to feel like an investigation you can continue, not a report you read once and abandon.

How RepoGhost works

The current project combines public GitHub data with AI-assisted analysis.

1. Investigate an account

Enter a GitHub username or organization, such as expressjs. RepoGhost retrieves the public profile and repository information.

2. Follow the evidence

Depending on the investigation, it can surface repository descriptions, programming languages, stars, forks, and visible activity. Repository-level investigations can also examine README files, sampled commits, issues, and releases when available.

3. Ask questions

The goal is to let you ask natural-language questions about the account and its projects, with answers grounded in the collected public evidence.

4. Follow the sources

Claims should lead back to the relevant public GitHub records. If the available information doesn't support an answer, RepoGhost should say what remains unknown rather than inventing a story.

The interesting engineering challenge: AI is not the source of truth

One lesson from building this project is that getting an AI model to return an answer is only part of the job.

The answer also needs to be relevant, concise, supported by evidence, and linked to valid sources.

Models can return malformed output, omit citations, or fail to answer the question directly. A fallback that simply dumps technical errors isn't useful to the person asking the question.

That's why I'm working on making RepoGhost more reliable: validating answers, checking citations against the actual evidence, handling model failures gracefully, and keeping verified GitHub data available even when AI inference fails.

I'd rather RepoGhost admit that it doesn't know than confidently tell someone something the evidence cannot support.

What RepoGhost should never pretend to know

Public GitHub data has limits.

Repository ownership doesn't prove that someone personally wrote every line of code. Recent activity doesn't prove code quality. Stars don't establish engineering ability. And public repositories cannot reveal someone's private work or personal motivations.

RepoGhost is intended to help people investigate evidence, not turn incomplete signals into unquestionable judgments.

Built in the open

I'm developing RepoGhost as part of my work around AI-powered developer tools and evidence-based software analysis.

The project is still evolving, and I'm treating the reliability issues as part of the engineering work—not something to hide behind a nice interface.

Try it with a GitHub account or organization you know. Ask what its projects do, inspect the sources, and see where the evidence leads.

👻 Try RepoGhost: https://repoghost.onrender.com

⭐ Explore the source code: https://github.com/egbutaify2-ui/repoghost

I'd particularly value feedback on one question:

What would make you trust an AI tool that investigates GitHub accounts and explains what it finds?

I'm building toward that standard, one investigation at a time.

articles.title: Java Erases Your Generics. TypeScript Erases Every Type. What Survives to Runtime
articles.description: Java keeps classes and generic signatures in bytecode. TypeScript keeps almost nothing. Which JVM habits break, and what replaces them.
articles.body_html:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

If you have written Java for a while, you have hit this wall at least once. You type list instanceof ArrayList<Integer> and the compiler refuses. The Oracle generics tutorial gives the reason in one line: "The runtime does not keep track of type parameters, so it cannot tell the difference between an ArrayList and an ArrayList."

You learned to live with it. You use ArrayList<?>, you pass a Class<T> around, you reach for Jackson's TypeReference when a List<User> has to come out of JSON.

Then you move to TypeScript, write if (value instanceof User) against an interface, and get 'User' only refers to a type, but is being used as a value here (a walkthrough of that error). Same family of problem, much bigger blast radius. Java erases your generics. TypeScript erases every type you write. The useful question is what is still there when the program runs, in each language, and what you do about the gap.

What javac erases, and what it quietly keeps

The Java tutorial on type erasure lists three things the compiler does: it replaces every type parameter with its bound, or Object if it has none; it inserts casts where they are needed for type safety; and it generates bridge methods so polymorphism still works in generic subclasses. The result, in the tutorial's words, is bytecode that "contains only ordinary classes, interfaces, and methods."

Take three lines:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("ada");
String first = names.get(0);

Run javap -c on the compiled class and the call to get goes to the erased List, whose get returns Object. The String you see in your source survives only as the cast the compiler inserted after the call. List<String> and List<Integer> run as the same class.

That is the part every JVM developer knows. The part people forget is how much Java keeps.

First, every object knows its own class. The TypeScript team's own guide for Java and C# programmers puts it plainly: in Java "any given value or object has one exact type", and you can call value.getClass() to ask for it.

Second, declarations keep their generics. The class file format has a Signature attribute that "stores a signature for a class, interface, constructor, method, field, or record component whose declaration in the Java programming language uses type variables or parameterized types." javap -v prints the Signature attribute, and reflection reads them: Field.getGenericType() must return a Type that "accurately reflect[s] the actual type arguments used in the source code."

Neal Gafter, who introduced super type tokens in a 2006 post, summed it up in a reply in that post's comments: "The STATIC types are recorded in the bytecodes, but not the dynamic types." A List<String> object has forgotten its String. A field declared as List<String> has not.


Java forgets the type arguments on values but keeps classes and declared signatures. TypeScript keeps neither.

What tsc erases: everything that is only a type

TypeScript's handbook has a section literally named Erased Types, and it ends on a note: "Type annotations never change the runtime behavior of your program."

Here is a small file with the usual suspects:

interface User { id: string; email: string }
type Users = User[];

function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined {
  return xs[0];
}

class Mailer {
  send(to: User): string {
    return `mail to ${to.email}`;
  }
}

Strip what is TypeScript-only and this is the JavaScript that remains (with a modern target, so the template literal stays as is):

function first(xs) {
  return xs[0];
}

class Mailer {
  send(to) {
    return `mail to ${to.email}`;
  }
}

User is gone. Users is gone. T is gone, with no Object stand-in and no inserted cast. The parameter annotation on send is gone. What survives is what was already JavaScript: the function and the class. The guide for OOP programmers says of an interface that it "is not present in any form at runtime", and that "information about e.g. the instantiation of a generic type parameter is not available at runtime." There is no Signature attribute equivalent. Nothing is recorded on the declaration either.

There is one opt-in way to record something: with emitDecoratorMetadata, tsc records a decorated member's type as a runtime reference, and NestJS dependency injection reads it. It records Array for a User[] and Object for an interface, so the generic and the interface are still gone.

Two TypeScript features do leave runtime code. Enums "are real objects that exist at runtime". The handbook shows enum Enum { A } compiling to an object with both directions mapped:

"use strict";
var Enum;
(function (Enum) {
    Enum[Enum["A"] = 0] = "A";
})(Enum || (Enum = {}));

const enum goes the other way: members are inlined at the use site and the declaration is "completely removed during compilation." Namespaces with values and constructor parameter properties also emit code.

That short list is shrinking in practice. Node.js now runs .ts files by stripping types by default since v22.18.0 and v23.6.0. It "will replace TypeScript syntax with whitespace, and no type checking is performed," and it rejects enums, namespaces with runtime code and parameter properties because those need a transform. TypeScript 5.8 added --erasableSyntaxOnly so the compiler flags the same constructs. TypeScript is drifting toward JavaScript plus annotations a runtime can delete.

Side by side:

At runtime Java TypeScript
Class of an object yes, getClass() only if built with new from a class
Generic args on a declaration yes, Signature attribute no
Generic args on a value no no
Interfaces yes, as class files no
Type aliases n/a no
Enums yes yes, unless const enum

Four Java habits that stop working

Overloading by type. Java lets you write describe(Card c) and describe(Iban i) as two methods and let the compiler pick. The TypeScript handbook on overloads describes something else: several overload signatures followed by a single implementation, whose signature "is not visible from the outside." There is one function body at runtime. If the two cases need different logic, that body has to look at the value and branch. (Java has its own edge here, by the way: you cannot overload print(Set<String>) and print(Set<Integer>), because the tutorial notes they "would all share the same classfile representation.")

instanceof on an interface. In Java, interfaces compile to class files and obj instanceof Payable works. In TypeScript the interface has no runtime value, so the check does not compile. And instanceof on a class only walks the prototype chain. The guide is blunt that typeof and instanceof "are still working on the values as they exist in the type-erased output code." An object from JSON.parse that has every field of Account is still not an instanceof Account.

Reflection on generic parameters. There is no getGenericType() to call. A function like load<T>(key: string): T cannot look at T, so whatever it returns, the T is only the caller's promise; nothing checks it. A super type token has nothing to capture, because the declaration carries no signature.

Deserialization by class. Jackson's model is mapper.readValue(json, User.class), plus new TypeReference<List<Integer>>() { } for the generic cases, which works because of that Signature attribute. In TypeScript, User is usually an interface, so there is no User.class to hand to anything. Even if you make it a class, a nested User[] field has no element type recorded anywhere for a library to read.


Classes and enums make it through compilation. Interfaces, type aliases and generics do not.

What replaces them: put the type information in a value

Every replacement follows one rule. If you need to know something at runtime, it has to exist at runtime as a value. TypeScript then checks that value statically.

Discriminated unions replace overloads and class hierarchies. Give each case a literal field and switch on it. The narrowing chapter defines it: "When every type in a union contains a common property with literal types, TypeScript considers that to be a discriminated union."

type Payment =
  | { kind: "card"; last4: string }
  | { kind: "iban"; iban: string };

function describe(p: Payment): string {
  switch (p.kind) {
    case "card":
      return `card ending ${p.last4}`;
    case "iban":
      return `transfer from ${p.iban}`;
  }
}

The kind string is the runtime tag Java gave you for free with getClass(). You write it yourself, and the compiler narrows p in each branch.

User-defined type guards replace instanceof on interfaces. A function whose return type is a type predicate, parameterName is Type, tells the compiler what a true result proves:

function isUser(v: unknown): v is User {
  if (typeof v !== "object" || v === null) {
    return false;
  }
  const u = v as Record<string, unknown>;
  return typeof u.id === "string"
    && typeof u.email === "string";
}

The catch: the compiler trusts the predicate. If the body checks the wrong fields, nothing warns you. Keep guards short and next to the type they guard.

Runtime schemas replace readValue(json, User.class). This flips the direction. In Java you declare the class and the deserializer reads it. In TypeScript you declare a schema, which is a real runtime value, and derive the static type from it. With Zod, now on major version 4, that looks like this:

import { z } from "zod";

const User = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  email: z.string(),
});
type User = z.infer<typeof User>;

const result = User.safeParse(JSON.parse(body));
if (result.success) {
  console.log(result.data.email);
}

safeParse returns either the data or an error instead of throwing, and z.infer gives you the User type for the rest of the code. You write the declaration once and get both a runtime validator and a compile-time type. That is the closest thing TypeScript has to a reified class, and it works for nested arrays and unions, which is where User.class ran out on the JVM too.

A habit to keep instead

The JVM taught you to trust declared types at the boundary because the runtime would back them up with a ClassCastException. TypeScript will not. At every boundary where data enters (HTTP bodies, queue messages, localStorage, environment variables) the static type is only as true as the check you ran. Inside the boundary, after a schema or a guard has passed, the types are as reliable as Java's.

Inside your code, write types and let them vanish. At the edges, write values that check.

If this was useful

Erasure is one of those differences that looks like trivia until it breaks a habit you have had for ten years. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript is the book I wrote for that move. It walks a JVM developer through what changes on the way over: variance, null safety, sealed classes into unions, coroutines into async/await. It is part of The TypeScript Library:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

If you come from Java or Kotlin, start with book 3 in place of book 1, then go to The TypeScript Type System when the generics get deep. If you ship TypeScript at work, add TypeScript in Production.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: What Hermes is fast at, and what it isn't
articles.description: React Native doesn't run your JavaScript on V8 or JavaScriptCore. It runs it on Hermes, an engine...
articles.body_html:
React Native doesn't run your JavaScript on V8 or JavaScriptCore. It runs it on Hermes, an engine Meta built for phones. I'd read the claims, fast startup and low memory, but never seen numbers on code that looks like an app's, next to an engine I know. So I built the exact Hermes that React Native 0.88 ships and ran the same scripts on it and on Node.

The short version: Hermes starts in a fraction of the time and uses a fraction of the memory, it keeps up with V8 on JSON, and it's two to five times slower than V8 at most other things, with regex replacement as the worst case I found.

The setup

  • Hermes 1.0.0, built from the hermes-v260318099.0.5 tag, which is the hermes-compiler version React Native 0.88.1 depends on. Release build, bytecode version 99.
  • Node 24.7.0 with V8 13.6, run normally and with --jitless.
  • An Apple M4 MacBook Air on macOS 26.3.1.

The --jitless runs matter. iOS doesn't let apps generate machine code at runtime, so no JavaScript engine in an iOS app gets a JIT. V8 with its JIT turned off is closer to what's actually possible on a phone than normal Node. Hermes doesn't use a JIT either. This build has a -Xjit flag, but it answers "JIT is not enabled in this build".

Hermes ran each script two ways: from source, and from bytecode compiled ahead of time with hermesc -O -emit-binary, which is what a React Native release build ships. Every test ran 7 times as a separate process. The tables show medians, and the spread was a few percent at most.

Starting up

Three scripts: one that only prints, lodash (544 KB, the full commented build), and a 5.4 MB file made of ten copies of lodash, each in its own function scope, to stand in for a large app bundle. Times are for the whole process, start to exit.

Script Node Node --jitless Hermes, source Hermes, bytecode
print only 24.8 ms, 42 MB 25.7 ms, 41 MB 5.3 ms, 9 MB 5.2 ms, 8 MB
lodash 28.4 ms, 50 MB 31.6 ms, 48 MB 122.8 ms, 34 MB 5.6 ms, 9 MB
5.4 MB bundle 68.6 ms, 98 MB 71.9 ms, 97 MB 1,580 ms, 200 MB 9.0 ms, 13 MB

This is what Hermes was built for. From bytecode, the large bundle started in 9 ms and the process peaked at 13 MB. Node took 69 ms and 98 MB.

From source it's the opposite. Hermes compiled the 5.4 MB bundle at startup, which took 1.6 seconds and 200 MB. V8 is far better at that, because it parses lazily and only compiles a function when it's called. So Hermes only makes sense with bytecode compiled ahead of time, which React Native does for release builds. In development, the app runs from source, and a slow start in debug mode doesn't tell you much about release.

Running app-like code

Four workloads, written the way app code usually looks:

  • JSON: parse and stringify a 5.6 MB feed response, 20,000 posts with nested users, tags and locations
  • list: filter, map and sort 100,000 posts, like preparing data for a long list
  • strings: build email addresses with toLowerCase and a regex replace, validate them, pull dates apart with a regex, build display labels with template literals
  • objects: create 300,000 small class instances and map them to props objects

Times are per iteration, measured inside the script. Bytecode and source ran at the same speed here, so I show the bytecode numbers.

Workload Node Node --jitless Hermes
JSON parse, 5.6 MB 16.0 ms 14.4 ms 14.8 ms
JSON stringify 13.4 ms 13.4 ms 11.6 ms
list 19.6 ms 39.0 ms 82.4 ms
strings 12.6 ms 35.6 ms 62.8 ms
objects 26.2 ms 49.6 ms 56.2 ms

JSON is the one place Hermes kept up. Parsing was level with V8, slightly faster than normal Node and slightly slower than --jitless, and stringifying was about 13% faster than either. That's not a small thing. Parsing API responses is a big part of what an app's JavaScript does.

Everywhere else, Hermes was two to five times slower than V8 with its JIT: about twice as slow creating objects, four times for the list and five for the strings. It was slower than V8 without a JIT too, by about 13% for objects and by about twice for the list and the strings. So "Hermes is fast" is true for startup and not for running code. For most screens that's fine, because 80 ms to sort 100,000 items isn't something you'd do on every frame. For anything heavy, it's a reason to keep the work small or move it to native code.

Memory

Peak resident memory for the whole process, same runs:

Workload Node Node --jitless Hermes
JSON 189 MB 214 MB 109 MB
list 219 MB 264 MB 122 MB
strings 146 MB 139 MB 42 MB
objects 306 MB 355 MB 123 MB

Hermes used between 29% and 58% of the memory normal Node did for the same work. On a phone, where the OS kills apps that use too much, that matters more than a few milliseconds.

Where the strings time went

The strings workload was the worst ratio, so I took it apart. 50,000 short names, each operation timed separately:

Operation Node Node --jitless Hermes
toLowerCase() 0.6 ms 1.8 ms 2.4 ms
replace(/\s+/g, ".") 3.2 ms 10.5 ms 33.4 ms
replace(/\s+/, ".") 1.6 ms 4.5 ms 14.4 ms
replaceAll(" ", ".") 4.5 ms 5.7 ms 11.0 ms
template literal 0.6 ms 3.0 ms 4.6 ms

toLowerCase and template literals were fine. Regex replacement was the slow part: Hermes took three times as long as V8 without a JIT, and ten times as long as normal V8. A plain-string replaceAll was three times faster than the regex version on Hermes, though it only matches single spaces, so it's not a drop-in replacement. If a hot path in your app runs a regex over every item in a list, that's the first thing I'd look at.

Bytecode is bigger than your minified source

Bytecode starts fast, but it isn't small:

JavaScript Hermes bytecode
lodash, full build with comments 544 KB 185 KB
lodash, minified 73 KB 186 KB
lodash, minified, gzipped 26 KB 97 KB

Against the commented source, bytecode looks three times smaller. Against the minified file, which is the fair comparison, it's two and a half times bigger, and almost four times bigger after gzip. So shipping bytecode trades download size for startup time. For most apps that's the right trade, but it's worth knowing which side the bill lands on.

What I got wrong

My first size comparison used the full lodash.js, and bytecode came out three times smaller. Most of that file is comments. Against the minified build, bytecode is much bigger, which is the opposite conclusion.

I expected to test Hermes's JIT too. The flag exists, but this build doesn't include the JIT, and React Native doesn't turn it on, so every Hermes number here is the interpreter.

And the first time I loaded lodash in Node, my script said lodash wasn't there. It was, but lodash saw Node's module object and exported itself through that instead of setting a global. I hid module and exports inside the wrapper, the same way the big bundle already did.

Caveats

This is a laptop, not a phone. An M4 is much faster than a mid-range Android phone, so the absolute numbers will be several times higher on a real device. The ratios between engines are what I'd trust, and even those could shift on a different CPU. Node isn't an engine you'd ship in an app; it's here as a reference point for V8. I didn't test JavaScriptCore, which is what React Native used on iOS before Hermes. The 5.4 MB bundle is ten copies of one library, so its bytecode deduplicated well and the 1.0 MB bytecode size for it isn't typical. Times include starting the process, which is part of why the empty script is in the table. And the workloads are mine. Your app's code might lean on something I didn't test.

What I'd take from it

  • Always ship Hermes bytecode in release builds. From source, Hermes took 1.6 s to start the large bundle. From bytecode it took 9 ms.
  • Don't judge startup in a debug build, because that runs from source.
  • Hermes is fast at JSON, so parsing big responses in JavaScript is fine.
  • Ordinary JavaScript runs several times slower than you'd see in Chrome or Node. Benchmark heavy loops on Hermes, not in the browser.
  • Watch regex in hot paths. replace with a regex was the slowest thing I measured.
  • Expect the bytecode to be bigger than your minified bundle, and budget app size for it.

articles.title: There's no more labagent.tech spam or phishing on dev.to. Here's how it got removed.
articles.description: Two weeks ago, every post I read had the same comment underneath it. Vietnamese text, on-topic,...
articles.body_html:
Two weeks ago, every post I read had the same comment underneath it. Vietnamese text, on-topic, ending with a link to labagent.tech. Click it and you got a fake dev.to login page asking for your credentials.

That's phishing. Not spam, not self-promotion — a fake login page designed to steal accounts.

Today, there's none. I checked. The scanner I run every night came back with zero reportable findings for the third day in a row. No labagent.tech, no tr.ee impersonation accounts, no phishing campaign against dev.to users.

Here's what happened.

What is Tiger Sentinel

Tiger Sentinel is a Python script that scans dev.to's public API for coordinated spam and phishing comments.

The concept came from Harun (@koda2026), a 12-year-old developer who built the original version to protect his own posts. I expanded it into a full daily scan that covers thousands of articles per run.

The name comes from Harun. The expansion is mine. The bot runs on GitHub Actions at 3 AM UTC every day.

What it does

For each article on dev.to, it fetches the comment thread and scores every comment against two tiers of signals.

Strong signals — two or more means "report this":

  • Known phishing domains (labagent.tech, suppdev.io)
  • Two or more impersonation phrases ("official platform update", "verify your account", "you have 24 hours")
  • Shortlink domain + Vietnamese text
  • Shortlink domain + near-empty comment
  • Shortlink domain + bot-style username (name_name_hexid)

Weak signals — flags for review, not report:

  • Single shortlink
  • Single impersonation phrase
  • Boilerplate phrases

A comment needs two strong signals to be classified as reportable. One strong signal plus weak signals lands in the review queue. Zero strong signals means ignore.

That's the whole design. The first version flagged every comment with a link at the end — 313 findings, most of them legitimate. The rewrite requiring two strong signals dropped the noise to near zero.

What it found

First full scan: 500 articles, 313 flags, 4 confirmed phishing accounts.

  • @anh_nguynvn_0478e614ba — 16 comments, labagent.tech
  • @shieldxbot — 12 comments, labagent.tech
  • @suppdevbot — 8 comments, tr.ee + "official platform update"
  • @devantibot — 9 comments, tr.ee + "verify your account"

All four created on the same day. All four posting the same pattern. That's not four spammers who found the same domain. That's a coordinated phishing campaign.

The bot also groups findings by shortlink domain, which turned 4 accounts into a larger picture:
tr.ee — 2 accounts (phishing)
labagent.tech — 2 accounts (phishing)
tinyurl.com — 25 accounts (coordinated?)
shorturl.at — 23 accounts (coordinated?)
t.co — 20 accounts (likely legitimate)

text

The tr.ee and labagent.tech pairs were the actual phishing campaign. The rest were pattern matches that needed human judgment.

How it got reported

dev.to has a report abuse form at /report-abuse that accepts bulk reports. I sent one submission:

  • The 4 confirmed phishing accounts
  • The 3 domain clusters
  • A note explaining which were confirmed phishing and which were pattern matches

Not 199 individual reports. One form, five groups. That's the difference between a report a moderation team can act on and a report that gets filed as noise.

What happened

A few days later, all four phishing accounts were gone. dev.to banned them. The tr.ee cluster dropped from 5 accounts to 3. labagent.tech disappeared entirely.

Two weeks later, my account was flagged as Trusted User. The system recognized that my report got a real phishing campaign removed. Trusted User status means future reports go to the front of the moderation queue.

What the scanner looks like now

Three full scans in a row have found zero reportable findings. The bot runs for five hours, covers roughly 5,000 articles per run, and comes back with nothing.

That's the success case. Not "the bot found more phishing." The bot finding nothing means the phishing campaign is gone and no new one has appeared.

The review findings — 900 to 1,000 per scan — are legitimate comments with shortlinks. People sharing tweets, blog posts, YouTube videos. Not phishing.

The cluster counts still fluctuate: t.co has 137 accounts, shorturl.at has 45. Those are likely legitimate. Twitter links and URL shorteners used by real users.

The lessons

The first version was wrong. 313 flags, mostly legitimate comments. The fix wasn't removing weak signals — it was requiring strong ones to co-occur.

The scanner is not a judge. It produces candidates. A human decides. The 313 → 4 funnel is the point. If a bot reports everything, it reports nothing.

Bulk beats individual. A moderation team processes "4 accounts using the same phishing domain" faster than 199 separate flags.

Continuous beats one-time. Daily scanning means the next phishing campaign gets caught on day one, not week three.

What's next

The bot runs every night. If a new phishing campaign appears, findings_report.json will have it in the morning. If a new cluster forms with a known phishing domain, the report goes to dev.to within a day.

The concept came from Harun. The daily scan is mine. The result is a platform with no active phishing campaign against it.

That's a real win. Not "I built a tool" — "I built a tool, used it, and the phishing campaign it was built to fix is gone."

The scanner is Python on GitHub Actions. I wrote it by describing what I wanted to Google AI Studio and fixing what broke. It's not production-grade — no tests, no retries on transient failures, no alerting. But it caught a real phishing campaign and got it removed.

Credit to Harun (@koda2026) for the original Tiger Sentinel concept. He built it to protect his own posts. I turned it into a daily scan.

The report abuse form at dev.to is /report-abuse. Bulk submission made the difference.

articles.title: I built a free calorie tracker with a metabolic safety floor. No card, no email, no paywall. And I found out why every other app doesn't.
articles.description: Every calorie app I tried had the same problem: it let you set a target of 1,200 calories or lower...
articles.body_html:
Every calorie app I tried had the same problem: it let you set a target of 1,200 calories or lower and called it a plan. Some went lower. That's how people end up in the binge-starve cycle — you eat 800, your body fights back, you eat 4,000, you hate yourself, repeat.

So I built one that refuses.

But here's the thing I figured out after two weeks of building it: the apps aren't badly designed. They're designed around a number you can't argue with.

The number that matters

Your BMR is the calories your body burns just staying alive. Mine is 1,396. If you eat below that for weeks, you don't just lose fat — you lose muscle. Your metabolism slows. The deficit that worked at 2,000 calories stops working at 1,400 because your body has adapted to the smaller intake.

Every app I tried let you set a target below your BMR anyway. Because the user asked. Because a lower number is a faster result. Because "it won't let me" is a support ticket.

ForkCount won't let you. It calculates your BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor), your TDEE (BMR × activity multiplier), and a target that keeps you above the BMR floor. If you try to set a target below that line, it refuses. You can override it in the settings, but the app tells you what you're doing and shows the maths.

That one decision — refusing to let the user hurt themselves — is the whole app. Everything else is a food diary.

What it does

A food diary that parses typed text. You type "200g chicken and 150g rice" and it becomes two items with macros. No database search, no barcode scan. Just type.

A weekly meal plan generator that respects your dietary preference. Set vegetarian, get vegetarian. Set vegan, get vegan. Set a calorie target of 1,400, get a plan built around 1,400 — not the default 2,000 that most generators quietly use.

A water tracker, weight log, exercise log with kcal estimates, and a community feed.

Free. No card. No trial. No paywall. Signup is a username, email, and password.

Stack

  • React + Vite + TypeScript
  • Supabase for database and auth (started on Firebase, migrated after the outage below)
  • GitHub Pages for hosting (deployed from docs/, not the repo root)
  • No backend. All logic is client-side.

The two bugs that taught me the most

Bug 1: The database disappeared.

I was on Firebase Firestore. One morning, every account was gone. Login failed. The app showed "user not found" for accounts that existed the day before. The Firestore API returned 404 NOT_FOUND: The database (default) does not exist for project.

It came back four hours later, untouched. Google had a backend issue. My data was fine. But for four hours, I thought I'd lost everything.

That's when I migrated to Supabase. Postgres. Real backups. No Google Cloud 2FA requirement. The migration took a weekend, and now the database is mine.

Bug 2: Firestore rejected undefined. Everywhere. Deeply.

Before the migration, the bug that cost me the most time was this:
Function setDoc() called with invalid data. Unsupported field value: undefined

text

Firestore refuses any document containing undefined anywhere inside it. Not null — undefined. And when it fails, it doesn't tell you which field. Just the document path. If you're saving a nested object with 40 fields, you're searching for a needle in a haystack.

The fix was a recursive cleaner routed through every write:


js
function cleanForFirestore(obj) {
  if (Array.isArray(obj)) return obj.map(cleanForFirestore);
  if (obj instanceof Date) return obj;
  if (obj && typeof obj === 'object') {
    const out = {};
    for (const k in obj) {
      if (obj[k] !== undefined) out[k] = cleanForFirestore(obj[k]);
    }
    return out;
  }
  return obj;
}
Then I wrapped setDoc, updateDoc, and addDoc in a safeFirestore helper that cleans the data before every write. One import change, and no write in the app can send undefined to Firestore again.

The lesson wasn't "fix the bug." It was "there is a class of bug, and you can kill the whole class with one wrapper."

The deploy lesson
The site broke for two days with this:

text
Failed to load module script: Expected a JavaScript-or-Wasm module script but the server responded with a MIME type of "application/octet-stream"
I was staring at the code. The problem was in GitHub Pages settings. It was serving my repo root — which has /src/main.tsx — instead of my built dist/ folder. The fix was to copy dist/ into a docs/ folder, point Pages at /docs, and stop letting it serve source.

The error message was the browser refusing to run a TypeScript file as JavaScript. Once you know that, it makes sense. The code was never broken. The deploy was.

What I'd like feedback on
Is the calorie calculation right? Mifflin-St Jeor for BMR, activity multiplier for TDEE, 300–500 deficit, floor at BMR. I want someone who actually knows nutrition math to sanity-check it. If the numbers are wrong, the app is wrong.

Does the onboarding flow make sense the first time you see it? Country → height/weight/age → fitness level → goal. Four steps. If it's confusing, I want to know where.

Does it break on your phone? I've tested on one device. I need more.

Does the meal plan respect your dietary preference? I fixed a bug where vegetarian users were getting turkey. If you set a diet and get a plan that violates it, that's a bug and I want to hear about it.

forkcount.github.io

I'm 13 and I built this by directing Google AI Studio, not by writing code by hand. So if something looks like a beginner mistake, it probably is. Tell me and I'll fix it.

articles.title: Chrome won't tell you when an extension is sold, so I built something that does
articles.description: You installed an extension three years ago. It does one small thing well, it has a few hundred...
articles.body_html:
You installed an extension three years ago. It does one small thing well, it has a few hundred thousand users, and you forgot it exists.

Then the developer sells it.

The buyer pushes an update. Chrome installs it silently in the background, like every update. The extension already has permission to read every page you visit, because it always had. Now it uses it: affiliate redirects, injected ads, or quietly shipping your browsing history somewhere.

This isn't hypothetical. It has happened many times to popular extensions, and the pattern is always the same. Nothing in Chrome tells you that the person behind an extension changed.

So I built Extension Guardian. It's free and open source. This post is about how it works and the one annoying problem I didn't expect.

What it watches for

Four signals catch most bad cases:

  1. The developer changed. The Chrome Web Store shows who offers each extension. If that name or email changes, the extension was probably sold.
  2. An update added permissions. Going from "read data on example.com" to "read data on all websites" deserves a warning.
  3. It vanished from the store. When Google finds malware, it usually removes the listing. Your installed copy keeps running, and nobody tells you.
  4. It came from outside the store. Extensions installed by another program or updating from a non-Google server are a classic adware trick.

Access is not risk

My first version had a problem: it rated almost everything "high". A password manager, an ad blocker and a grammar checker all need to read every page, because that's their job.

So every extension gets two separate ratings:

  • Access: what its permissions technically allow (full, limited, basic).
  • Risk: whether you should trust it.

Risk combines the warnings above with signals from the store page. Few users and no updates in two years raise it. A large user base, recent updates and a registered business lower it. Critical signals, like an owner change or removal from the store, always mean high risk, no matter how popular the extension is.

The scoring looks roughly like this:

score = critical * 40 + firm + Math.max(0, soft - good);
level = critical > 0 ? 'high' : score >= 40 ? 'high' : score >= 15 ? 'watch' : 'low';

"Soft" signals, like few users, can be offset by good ones. A recent jump in permissions is "firm" and can't be talked down by a big install count, because a big install count is exactly what a buyer pays for.

The surprise: extensions can't read the Chrome Web Store

The developer info lives on the public store page, so the plan was simple: fetch chromewebstore.google.com/detail/<id> from the extension and parse it.

Chrome blocks that. Extensions can't script or fetch the Web Store, even with host permissions. It's a deliberate protection, so a malicious extension can't install or review other extensions.

The fix is a tiny server. A Cloudflare Worker fetches the public page, extracts the developer name, email, user count and last update date, and returns JSON. Results are cached in Workers KV for 6 hours, so the store is hit rarely.

The extension sends only extension IDs, nothing about the user. IDs are public 32-letter identifiers, the same ones in every store URL. The server allows any origin through CORS, so the extension doesn't even need a host permission for it, and Chrome shows no extra install warning.

Parsing a page with no API

There's no official Web Store API for this, so the server parses HTML, which can break whenever Google changes the layout. Two safeguards:

  • Fixtures of real store pages in the tests, so a layout change shows up as a failing test, not as wrong data.
  • If more than half of a user's extensions suddenly come back "not found", the extension assumes the parser broke and doesn't raise removal alerts. A false "removed from store" alert on every extension would be worse than no alert.

Try it

  • Chrome Web Store
  • Source on GitHub

It's early, so the most useful feedback is false alarms: an extension you trust that it flags as risky, and why you trust it. Tuning those signals is most of the work.
